Skycity Convention Centre—Negotiation of Costs
12. Dr DAVID CLARK (Labour—Dunedin North) to the Minister for Economic

items.speaker: Development
items.text: What was the “range of price escalation” f or the New Zealand
International Convention Centre as recorded in advice to the Minister dated 26 February

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: As is clear in the
other released documents that were written around that same time, the figure was a net
$30 million to $40 million. It was the Government’s expectation at that time that any
additional costs would be, effectively, designed out in a subseq uent preliminary design
stage. As we all now know, the preliminary design came back on 15 October at a much
wider cost differential, and that was put into the public domain before the end of last
year.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Has he sought and re ceived a revaluation of the land Skycity
acquired from Television New Zealand for the purposes of building a convention centre
and upon which Skycity now intends to build a five -star 300-bedroom hotel; if not, why
not?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: No, I have not to this point, but I have made it clear in
response to questions from Green Party members that we will absolutely be taking into
account any changes that are to Skycity’s benefit and calculating that into the overall
value of the centre and what we will accept for the concessions that Parliament has
legislated for.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Can the Minister give an assurance that the originally proposed
column-free design for the large convention space will be retained?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: It is interesting—I collect a lot of criticism for designing it
personally and, obviously, in the instance I might not be designing the exact placement
of columns in the convention centre. Look, we will assess for the member, at the time,
the next iteration of the preliminary design, and the public will get the opportunity to
assess that, and we will all be able to decide whether that constitutes the international
convention centre that we are all seeking for Auckland.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: In light of that answer, did Skycity seek assurances he would not
be involved in the convention centre construction process, and was it because it was
concerned to avoid further “Gerry -mandering”, “John -mandering”, and “Joyce -
mandering”?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I have news for the member: I have no intention of being
involved in the construction of the convention centre. It is fair to say I am not the most
adept at carrying a hammer and wielding a hammer, but I would defer, of course, to my
friend Mr Brownlee, who does have some experience in that regard, but I can inform the
member he does not intend to be spending his time constructing the convention centre
either.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: I move, That the House take note
of miscellaneous business . Well, there is only one question that New Zealanders are
asking after the first few weeks of this political year, and that is: “When will the half -
truths, the double-speak, the dissembling, and the obfuscation come to an end?”. If there
25 Feb 2015 General Debate 1909
is one thing that these Government members have mastered, it is that they cannot tell it
straight. From the Prime Minister to the Minister for Economic Development to the
Minister of Finance, they cannot tell a straight story to New Zealand. They have to dress
it up. They have plenty to hide. They have plenty to conceal, and they have had plenty
opportunities to do so. But it is all coming to an end—it is all coming to an end.
It was very interesting hearing the “Minister for Construction of Casinos and Hotels”
just now, talking about the Skycity deal. It was another example —just another
example—of Government members having the chance to tell New Zealanders the full
truth, the chance to be upfront and straight -up with New Zealanders, and not being able
to do it. They could not do it. When they knew 15 months ago that they did not have the
money—that they might be ponied up for a bit more money because the poor old
gambling company Skycity could not afford it; it could not afford to make its promise—
Government members did not say a thing about it, and John Key and Steven Joyce
continued to promise that we would have a free convention centre.
Then Government members started the softeni ng-up act. They won the election and
they thought: “That’s it. We’re quids in here, brothers. We’ll soften them up, and they’ll
have no objection. We’ll tell them another $140 million —what am I bid? What am I
bid?”. They tried to soften us up but it did no t work. The people of New Zealand said:
“No—a promise is a promise.” When John Key, the great helmsman, says he makes a
promise, he should stick with it. It is an unusual occurrence, actually, for New
Zealanders to see the Prime Minister make a promise and  stick to it, but on this score,
this time, on this occasion they said: “No. He made the promise; he must stick to it.”
And so Government members were forced to back down. Of course, it was not the
Prime Minister, who had made the promise, who had to perfo rm the somersault. It was
left to the ever-agile and nubile Steven Joyce to do that. He had to perform the U-turn.
Then we have Donghua Liu’s story. This is a never -ending story. Before the election
National members thought they had it all sewn up. Their mate, their little mate, wrote
out a cheque for $25,000 and personally handed it to Jami -Lee Ross —personally
handed it to Jami -Lee Ross —who put it in his bank account and had it sitting there
earning interest at the sky -high rates that the Government keeps  telling us about.
Donghua Liu wrote them out a cheque and they thought they had it all over us. It was
like “Oh, the poor old Labour Party. Look, you wrote a letter. You had this.”
We had the allegation of a $100,000 bottle of wine. Nobody had heard of t he bottle
of wine. The affidavit that they claimed to be sworn was nowhere to be seen. The
written statement that followed the affidavit was nowhere to be seen. They had a thing
on a paper napkin that they then talked about. That could not be found either,  and it all
turned out to be just a load of old codswallop. But what was not codswallop was the
cosy relationship between the Prime Minister, John Key, and Donghua Liu —the man
now facing court charges. Oh, yes! It was not the mythical $100,000 bottle of wi ne; it
was the very real $25,000 cheque that found its way into the bank account of Jami -Lee
Ross, but they would not front up and tell us the truth at the time.
Then there is State housing. They are very important, State houses. Many New
Zealanders are d ependent on them because they cannot afford to buy their own. They
cannot afford to live within the private rental market. Was there one word spoken
during last year’s election campaign, where they promised they would sell off the State
houses? No way, and  they would not front up about that. And now we have the
deployment of troops to Iraq. Did they ever tell us that 16 personnel would be sent up
there for training, with 106 sent to provide security? Did they ever tell us that they
would be within spitting distance of the front line of the Islamic State? They would not
tell us that, either.
1910 General Debate 25 Feb 2015
They cannot tell the story straight—they cannot tell the story straight—and now they
cannot be straight about how long those personnel will be there. This is not a job t hat
will take 2 years. This is a long-term job dealing with one of the most evil organisations
in the world, and we have a Prime Minister who cannot be straight with New
Zealanders about exactly what the Government is committing good New Zealand troops
to. They will not tell us everything. They will not tell us what the facts are. They will
stand up here in the comfort of their leather armchairs and accuse others of not having
courage, but they do not have the courage to front up to New Zealanders.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I
seek leave to table a photograph showing the Hon Rick Barker handing over the
$100,000 bottle of wine to Donghua Liu’s partner.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That will not help the order of this House.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I have sought leave.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Oh, the member has sought leave; that is true . Leave is sought to
table that particular document. Is there any objection? There is.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I am delighted to stand and
contribute to this general debate. I want to do so on the basis of discussing what kind of
country we are, what sort of leadership we are entitled to expect, what sorts of values
we want to see inculcated in our young people, how we provide that, and the sort of
leadership that  is available to them. Yesterday the Prime Minister exhibited all those
values. We are a country that plays its part. We are small. We are distant. We are
descended from people who were great adventurers and navigators, who crossed the
Pacific looking for something better, and who were prepared to build that something
better, but in so doing recognise that we have links across this world. We are part of a
community that is connected and linked, and we are bringing up children in this society
who understand that connectedness, who want to continue the traditions of our country
of travel, of meeting other people, and of being safe to explore and go on adventures.
That means that we do have to be aware and wary of many of the risks and dangers that
characterise the world that our young people are growing up in.
We also want to make sure that they understand the history that they are descendants
from. Before them there have been many New Zealanders who have gone into theatres
of war, who have seen that defining our belief of what the quality of citizenship is in
this country. It is important that we continue to not only maintain the respect for those
traditions that are invoked on Anzac Day and in the year of the commemoration of the
100th anniversary of Gallipoli but keep that responsibility current.
The Prime Minister, in announcing yesterday the decision of the Government that we
would continue to play our part, is continuing to invoke that pride of citizenship that is
so important to us and to who we are as N ew Zealanders and as Kiwis. I for one am
personally absolutely committed to that direction. I for one am one of those young
people—well, actually, I am not that young. In comparison to some of my colleagues on
the other side of the House, I probably am. Bu t, certainly, I grew up going to dawn
ceremonies on Anzac Day in Ruatōria and now in Wellington. I grew up with the names
of heroes and heroines on our war memorials and in our marae around this country.
Now I am a proud chair of the Ngārimu VC and 28th (M āori) Battalion Memorial
Scholarship Fund Board, which invokes all of those memories. The people who joined
those battalions, and who join our Defence Force today, joined knowing that they want
to be able to have that opportunity. The whole point, by defin ition, of having a defence
force is that they are training to carry out those responsibilities. So we cannot on the one
hand evoke the emotion of turning up to Anzac Day and then turn away from the actual
practical reality of what that means. No, this Gove rnment is not prepared to do that, and
25 Feb 2015 General Debate 1911
this Prime Minister has demonstrated the courage, the wisdom, and also the great belief
in who we are to take that stand.
As the Minister of Education, I consider that critical for young New Zealanders,
because we have a curriculum that says to them that these are the values of who we are.
We play our part. We want them to be travellers. We want them to be explorers. We
want them to be mindful of risk. We want them to be relationship developers. We want
them to be com municators. And we should not turn away as a nation when that
responsibility looks us in the face and says: “Will you stand alongside the allies whom,
in times of both war and trade, we look to for those relationships?”. So, no, this
Government will not tu rn away from those responsibilities, and it is important that not
only we confront them in a timely fashion but we demonstrate to young New
Zealanders that that is part of who we are. We are descended from people who played
their part, who took the risks, and who were prepared to do what was necessary. And so,
as the Minister of Education, I believe that our schools are playing their part and are
making those contributions. We have invested in connectedness. We have invested in
ensuring that young people ca n critically think —critically think —and analyse what
their responsibilities are.
We are seeing progress in our education system, and that, actually, should reassure
all of us that we are continuing to build a strong nation, and a nation that is being led by
a Government and a Prime Minister who understands that we must govern not just for
now and the immediate future but for our future and our ability to hold our heads high.
That is why New Zealand got such a big vote to go on to the United Nations Securit y
Council. It is because we are recognised for our integrity and for the part we play. So I
am proud to stand alongside our Prime Minister, our Government, and the decision that
has been made to continue this responsibility as New Zealanders.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: Well, I guess today’s paper pretty much sums it up, if you
look at the front page of the Dominion Post . On the right -hand side you have
photographs and a story about the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria  (ISIS): “ISIS fight:
Key fired up”—or not, apparently; and “Emphatic no for the super -city in voter poll”. I
want to speak briefly about both these issues. I think probably the one part of the front
page of the Dominion Post that I would like the members of the Government to focus
on is the part here with United States journalist Steven Sotloff standing beside —that is
“Jihadi John”, is it not?

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Kneeling beside.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: Kneeling beside “Jihadi John”. The question that I have  for this

items.speaker: Government is
items.text: what is your contingency plan? If one of our soldiers ends up in an
orange jumpsuit beside “Jihadi John”, what is your plan? Will you pay the ransom, will
you send in the SAS, or will you stand by and allow one of our soldiers to b e beheaded?
That is the real question, and I have not heard anything from this Government. And I
put it to this Government: before the troops go—

items.speaker: Hon Paul Goldsmith
items.text: It could happen tomorrow, you great goof.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: Do not make light of it, silly Mr—what is your name?

items.speaker: Barbara Stewart
items.text: Goldsmith.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: Goldsmith. Do not make light of this. See, the thing I know about
people in Parliament —and I used to say this to Keith Locke —is that most often the
people who have the loudest voices when it comes to deploying people into theatres of
war are those who have never worn a uniform and never want to. And very, very often,
sadly, you find that they do not allow their sons or daughters to go either. So b utton it,
Mr Goldsmith —button it. You have no place commenting on this because, quite
frankly, you do not know what you are sending troops to.
1912 General Debate 25 Feb 2015
The other point I want to talk about is the Local Government Commission and the
super-city amalgamation. As the Mayor of Carterton I tried to have conversations with
various Government Ministers and a range of people —indeed, yourself, Mr Speaker
when you were the Minister of Local Government —and I tried to impress upon people
what was going to happen. I know this Go vernment passed legislation to make it easier
to force amalgamations, and it has relied on the Local Government Commission to put
together the necessary papers to effect that. That is the aspiration. We know that. But
what we have right now is two things: an incompetent Local Government
Commission—and I did ask the Minister of Local Government whether she had
confidence in it. She said yes. The trouble is that since the commission’s Wellington
proposal has been released, it has had to make three corrections  of fact, and there is still
one major glaring error of fact in its proposal where it has estimated the costs of
merging the Wairarapa councils’ IT systems into one at $25 million —wrong. The three
Wairarapa councils have been doing that work for the last 5  years, and had the
commission bothered to pick up the phone and ring one of the chief executive officers
over there it would have been told that the cost was probably about $1.5 million to
polish it off —$1.5 million, not $25 million. I am sorry, but the L ocal Government
Commission reeks of incompetence.
And now we have an amazing statement, a ruling coming out of the Broadcasting
Standards Authority, which has found that the Greater Wellington Regional Council and
Fran Wilde have lied—lied—in their marketing propaganda to the people of the Greater
Wellington region. I have got to hand it to Stephen Franks, who has taken Fran Wilde
and the Greater Wellington Regional Council to task, and the councillors of the Greater
Wellington Regional Council, and is ask ing them, as honest members of the council:
“How do you feel about this? Will you seek an inquiry into the Greater Wellington
Regional Council’s propaganda?”. I stand here ready to assist this Government to a
sensible solution for the Wairarapa, which is a unitary authority, and it would help if the
local member stood up for his people as well. But we are not going to lie down and let
this Government and the Local Government Commission allow the people of the
Wairarapa to be forced into a Wellington super -city when 85 percent of them do not
want it.

items.speaker: Hon Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: Xin nian Kuai le. Gong
xi fa cai. Sun nin fail lok. Gong hay fat choy, and a happy New Year, a happy lunar
New Year, to you, Mr Speaker. Over the past few weeks I have been attending functions
throughout my electorate and across this country to celebrate the lunar New Year.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: You haven’t.

items.speaker: Hon Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: I have not seen Mr Peters there, and we know why
he does not turn up at these functions, but these events culminated last n ight with a
function that I hosted here in Parliament that you, Mr Speaker, attended. The one thing
that these events draw together is that they remind us that New Zealand is a place where
cultures can thrive and flourish. Different heritages and languages  are part of the
thriving web of interaction that is our country, one that we all love and admire. We
know it is the Year of the Sheep, and of course many in this country have close
associations to these fine animals, including you, as a former sheep farme r, Mr Speaker.
For me there is a rich history of sheep in this country: 39 million out there today. I think
that, based on that, this will be New Zealand’s year, the Year of the Sheep. People born
under this sign are known to be creative and resilient, and to persevere.
That can best describe the role of this National Government in 2015. This country is
going into this year in good shape: resilient and strong. Our Prime Minister leads a
Government that has stabilised this economy. It grew 3.2 percent last year, and average
wages have grown 15 percent over the last 5 years, and are forecast to head even faster
25 Feb 2015 General Debate 1913
into the future. Employment is strong. As the Minister for Economic Development,
Steven Joyce, has said, 80,000 more people are now employed than a ye ar ago—80,000
more people. There are 217,000 more—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Unemployment is still higher than when Labour was in office.

items.speaker: Hon Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: —people employed than 5 years ago. And how do I
know that? I say to Mr Clark, come to Maungakiekie, come talk to the employers that
actually create jobs, wealth, and opportunities for our people and our communities, and
they are saying to me that they want to hire more people, that they are growing, and
they are confident that this Government is delivering for them.

items.speaker: Unemployment remains low
items.text: 5.7 percent. This is forecast to drop down to 4.5
percent. Some of the things I am proud of about this Government is that, in terms of my
role as Minister for Pacific Peoples , we now have 116,300 Pacific people employed,
and that is the most at any time in our history —the most at any time in our history. We
know that meaningful long -term employment is the best way not just for Pacific
families but for all families to succeed a nd thrive in this country. These positive
statistics reflect that more young people are in jobs, gaining qualifications, and moving
into sustainable, higher-paying jobs. That is what the people of Maungakiekie expect of
this Government, and that is what Pacific people are now reaping the benefits of in such
a positive economy.
As the Minister of Corrections, I am focused on reducing reoffending by 25 percent
by 2017. We all know that the crime rate is at its lowest in three decades, but there are
still too  many people reoffending. We are taking measures through education
programmes and rehabilitation programmes in our prisons, and also through converting
every prison in this country to a working prison. Why? Because we know that
employment is the best way o ut of poverty, the best way out of welfare, and the best
way to stay out of our prisons. We know also that specialist aftercare services are being
promoted in our prisons, and we are working hard to deliver on drug and alcohol
rehabilitation programmes, which are heavily placed in our prisons.
Lastly, can I just say that I am 100 percent behind our Government’s decision to
stand alongside its allies and fight this evil organisation that calls itself the Islamic State
of Iraq and the Levant. It poses one of  the biggest threats to this world since World War
II, and we must do whatever we can to defeat it. We cannot ignore the fact that we are
part of the international community, and there comes a point, as the Prime Minister said
yesterday, when we must stand  up and be counted. I am proud to be a New Zealander,
just like Mr Mark is. I am proud to be part of a Government that will not bow down to
the fear and terror of the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria, and I am proud that we have
made this decision to go to Iraq.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: Last night TV3’s Campbell Live showed
us a side of New Zealand that, frankly, made me sick to my stomach and should make
the National Government deeply ashamed. A class of 28 teenage girls at Kelston Girls’
College, a very nice west Auckland high school, were asked whether they had eaten
breakfast and what they had in their bags for lunch. The result was that 18 girls had no
lunch. That is right —18 out of  28 girls had nothing for their lunch, and eight of them
had had nothing for breakfast either. I find this hard to get my head around. Eighteen
girls are expected to learn, to focus, and to function well in their school for the whole
day, and to come away with National Certificate of Educational Achievement success at
the end of it, when they have got grumbling tummies and have had nothing to eat. I find
that staggering.
I would like to know something. Since when did the idea of classrooms full of
hungry kids become tolerable in a country like New Zealand? I just do not know what
else to make of the Government’s blasé response to the numbers of kids turning up to
1914 General Debate 25 Feb 2015
school without food, other than to assume that it thinks that that is OK. Well, I will tell
you what—kids going hungry for the whole day at school is not my new normal. Child
hunger in this country is a national emergency, and we today —today—can do
something about it.
Tonight it is likely my “Feed the Kids Bill” will come up in this House for debat e
and a vote. Before MPs vote on it, I just want to say this: there is no reason on earth not
to vote for my bill. If you do not like the idea of feeding kids lunch at school —if that
grates with your sensibilities —then vote the bill down at the second read ing or at the
third reading. Do not deny Parliament the first real opportunity we have had to sit down
with others across the political spectrum, with experts, with families, and with schools
to hear what the solutions are for this national emergency. That  is what you will be
doing if you vote the bill down. You will deny the House a unique and crucial
opportunity to put politics aside and do something for our kids who are in need.
I also want to say this to all MPs: when was the last time that you worked a  whole
day without having had anything to eat since breakfast? Do you think you could do your
job if you did not eat something at morning tea or lunchtime? We all know that
breakfast is not enough to get anyone through a whole day, so let us not pretend th at a
bowl of Weet-Bix in the morning is enough to see our kids through a whole school day
either. Kids need lunch—it is simple—like we all do.
Last night we heard from KidsCan and the principal of Kelston Girls’ College that
the problem of hunger in schoo ls is increasing every day. It is not —with respect to the
Prime Minister, who has not visited many low -decile schools—a problem for the odd
one or two.

items.speaker: Hon Anne Tolley
items.text: Stop making it up. That’s not true.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: No—Julie Chapman from KidsCan said that around 22 percent
of children in schools that she deals with are hungry every day. The number is up from
15 percent just a year earlier. Kelston Girls’ College is not an isolated story. The parents
of the girls love their kids just as much as anyone in this House loves their own kids, but
the school principals are saying the parents just do not have as much money.
It is a compassionate country that we live in —Aotearoa. We act before we judge
people. When the earthqua kes struck, we acted to help people without judgment or
favour. If a child falls over and is cut, we help them regardless of why they were hurt.
We act because we care for all the kids in this country. So today I am asking members
across this House to have  the guts to do what is really right and vote for the “Feed the
Kids Bill”. Hungry kids are not the new normal in this country. It is a national
emergency, and tonight we all have the chance to do something about it. Thank you.
Hon NICKY WAGNER (Associate Minister for Canterbury Earthquake
Recovery): It has been a significant week for New Zealand, and it is only Wednesday.
On Sunday we had the 4 th anniversary of the Canterbury earthquakes and yesterday we
made the commitment for our Defence Force to train in Iraq. Both provide us with an
opportunity to reflect on being a Kiwi, what we value in New Zealand, and why we
need to protect our people and our quality of life.
Rebuilding Canterbury so that it is a great place to live, work, and raise a family is
one of the Government’s priorities. The 4 th anniversary on Sunday gave us an
opportunity to take stock of how far we have come. There is a new normal in
Christchurch, in Canterbury. What we think about, what we care about, and what we do
is different now. People are more precious; things less so. We take pleasure in the small
things, like a smooth road —things that we took for granted in the past. We are  more
creative. We are more community -minded, and public spaces and events are more
popular.
25 Feb 2015 General Debate 1915
Physically, there is huge change in our area. When you look you can see building
everywhere. Roads are being repaired, houses are being built, and suburbs are bei ng
recreated. The central city, newly focused on a cleaned and restored Avon/Ōtākaro
River, is coming alive. The anchor projects are taking shape. Businesses and
organisations are returning to the town, and there is a real buzz of activity.
Everyone can s ee the physical rebuild, but what about the people of Canterbury?
Everyone has lost someone or something. Everyone has their own experience and their
own story, and everyone copes in a different way and in a different time frame. But as
the Associate Minis ter for Canterbury Earthquake Recovery, I am concerned about the
well-being of the community as a whole and how they feel about life. The latest
research, part of the All Right? campaign for greater Christchurch, tells us that fewer
people are now worried about having another big earthquake. Significantly fewer people
are dealing with the things that happened as a result of the earthquakes. But in terms of
well-being and community, respondents feel better connected to greater Christchurch
and more respondents reported regularly giving their time to help others.
When we compare Christchurch with the rest of New Zealand in the local
government Quality of Life Survey, we see that across the six cities 82 percent of
people rate their quality of life as positive , and in Christchurch that figure is 80 percent.
In those six cities 17 percent of people feel stressed most of the time, and in Canterbury,
that figure is 19 percent. But the statistic that I found the most interesting is that across
the six cities, people tell us that “they have someone to turn to for help if they are faced
with a serious illness or injury, or needed emotional support during a difficult time”. In
those six cities 92 percent of people feel that, but in Christchurch the figure is 94
percent of people. So we do stick together. We are supporting each other.
So we have made some progress but we have still got some way to go. But I think we
are seeing a benefit in that people feel engaged and are participating in our community.
Last weekend alo ne, as well as the memorial services in the city, we had a Cricket
World Cup match, a well -patronised fun run, and disabled surfing. The ethnic
communities had a soccer tournament and we had the Chinese New Year celebration,
and that all on top of our norm al events. Cantabrians are out and about and enjoying
themselves.
We are championing creativity and the arts in our rebuild. We have the Gap Filler
events, and recently we had the Spectrum Street Art Festival, which will make
Christchurch the leading city  for street art in New Zealand. We have restored the Isaac
Theatre Royal. We have got the Court Theatre running, and performances in Hagley
Park. There is something for everyone. While I am here I would like to draw the
attention of the House to the public consultation on the new earthquake memorial. From
an international call for ideas we got 330 proposals, and six of those have been chosen.
You can have your say online.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: Yesterday in the House was one of those rare
occasions when we saw some raw honesty from the Prime Minister —in his breathless
justification as to why we should send troops to Iraq. If the Prime Minister could ante
up yesterday, why could he not ante up befor e the election, when he made quite
different statements about his Government’s position on sending troops to Iraq? Before
the election it was a completely different story. Before the election Mr Key was quite
adamant that there would be no SAS or troop dep loyment to Iraq. He was telling people
before the election that this was National’s solid policy. Asked again whether he would
rule out deploying our special forces to Iraq, even in an advisory capacity, Mr Key said:
“I would say yes.”
Why are there two d ifferent stories from our Prime Minister? Before the election he
said that there was no way we were sending our troops to Iraq, not even in an advisory
1916 General Debate 25 Feb 2015
capacity, but yesterday in the House, he was breathlessly justifying sending troops to
Iraq as well as s ending troops in an advisory capacity. What happened? Why the lies?
Why the mistruth? Why the different story before the election, and why the story we got
yesterday—that we are in, boots and all?
Also, when that side of the House sends a message to this side of the House that we
are not supportive of our troops, I say that we will always be supportive of our troops
whenever they are sent anywhere. You can play politics and throw out that accusation
about us, but we will always support our troops. On this side of the House we do not
support the nature of what you are doing in Iraq, but we will always support any of our
troops and anyone in our Defence Force when they are sent out on a mission.
But there is a pattern for me here. Just like Mr Key softened the New Zealand public
up with sending troops to Iraq, there are half -truths and mistruths with him everywhere.
The Prime Minister made accusations about the Labour Party getting donations from
Donghua Liu when at the very same time he was going around to Mr Liu’s house for
dinner: “Come on in, John. Have a $25,000 cheque.” Have a $25,000 cheque. So it was
hypocritical for the Prime Minister to throw barbs at our side of the House when he was
going around for dinner. Mr Liu and Mr Key were sitting around the dinner table —but
no, Mr Key did not go around; he said that he just saw him at occasions and fundraisers.
Well, I am sorry, Mr Key, but the public does not buy your story that you saw Mr Liu a t
fundraisers and functions, because you went around to his house for tea. I certainly
would remember if I got invited around to someone’s house and then $25,000 arrived in
my bank account as a campaign donation. So I am sorry, Mr Key, but the public does
not buy it. The public does not buy your web of lies and web of deceit around Iraq or
around Mr Liu.
And, of course, there is another issue here, which is dear to my heart, and that is the
sale of State houses. There was not one mention of the mass sale o f State houses before
the election, but post-election, it is all on. There are 8,000 State houses on the chopping
block. What did Mr Key say about the sale of State houses before the election? He said
that the truth was there are not a lot of other assets that would fit the category where
they would be appealing to send to the market. But we know that at the same time his
Minister Nick Smith was talking to the Housing New Zealand Board and saying that the
Government expected that Housing New Zealand would o wn a significantly smaller
number of houses in 10 years’ time.
What I do not like about this is the way that this Government has dressed it up.
Hundreds of homes in my electorate were made vacant —the tenants kicked out —under
some kind of premise that it w as for earthquake strengthening. But that is not what was
going on. Those people were being kicked out of their homes for those properties to be
readied for sale. That is what was happening. A lot of them are still vacant, and the way
they have been looked  after—or have not been looked after —has caused crime in our
communities, and we will find out more about that. This Government has just left those
properties to deteriorate. It is deserting communities, and crime is happening in them.
This Government has sat around and done nothing with those houses. It had an agenda
of selling them off, but we did not hear about that before the election. We will hear
more about that later.
There are many, many other cases where this Government has told one story before
the election and another one afterwards, and the public are getting used to it.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: I want to start my contribution this
afternoon by acknowledging the pain of the Ōāmaru family who lost a daughter—a little
5-year-old girl; a sister, she had grandparents—as a result of a fatal accident at Moeraki,
just south of Ōāmaru. My heart goes out to them. My love and my sympathy are with
them. They are a well -known North Otago f amily. When a tragedy such as a fatal
25 Feb 2015 General Debate 1917
accident such as this one occurs, it goes further than just the immediate family —and,
God knows, they are feeling enough pain at this time —it goes right into the local
community and even more widely. I just want to say , as their local member of
Parliament, that I am absolutely backing the need for us to make all roads in New
Zealand safe for everyone.
The Upper Clutha and Otago area is a hot spot for fatalities and serious accidents
involving foreign drivers. The impact is felt not just in New Zealand but on the families
of the drivers from other countries around the world—the effects are felt there. I want to
acknowledge the work already done by this Government and by Government agencies
in their efforts to make New Ze aland roads and New Zealand driving conditions safer
for all drivers. I want to acknowledge the work of Ministers, who are very concerned
about this issue. I am concerned as the local member of Parliament, but I want to
acknowledge that they too are concer ned and that there is a considerable amount of
work going on to see whether we can make conditions for driving better in New
Zealand. I want to see more, however. I want to see closer attention on what more we
can do.
Is it that we can put in more yellow lines? Is it as simple as putting in more
directional arrows so that when somebody drives out of an intersection they do not find
themselves disorientated? If we can do that to make our roads safer for New Zealanders
and visitors alike, let us do it. Let us just do it. So this Government, and this Parliament,
is not sitting on its hands over this issue. There is a petition sitting before the Transport
and Industrial Relations Committee. I know that it has done a lot of work on this issue
and that it is abou t to hear a submission by a petitioner whom I support —young Sean
Roberts from Geraldine, who lost his father 3 years ago in a motorcycle accident. I
supported that petition into Parliament; I sponsored it into Parliament.
This Parliament is taking this is sue seriously. The select committee is doing
something about this issue. I have said this before in contributions in the House, but I
mean it, and I mean it from my heart. I want to see our roads in New Zealand made safe
for New Zealanders and visitors alike. On a happier note, in the few minutes—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Why is the Government not acting? Why does it keep delaying?

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: You see, there is a member from Dunedin North who should know
better. He should know that th is Government has done a significant amount of work on
making our roads safer. In the time of the previous Government we did not see
directional arrows, did we? As an Opposition MP, I had to cry against the wind to see
whether we could get these basic safe ty measures in place. That was during the Clark
Government. It had 9 years to make our roads safer. It took this Government to put the
investment into roading.
It took this Government to put the investment into educating our visitors to New
Zealand throug h the Tourism New Zealand website and through information on
aeroplanes coming into New Zealand. All these measures have happened under this
Government. Although the Opposition can sit back and cry doom, I ask those members
to look inside their hearts and ask what they did to fix this problem, and contrast that
with what is happening now. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: Getting the whole truth out of the Prime Minister
is like pulling teeth.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: Oh rubbish!

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: “Rubbish!”, he says. There goes the man who used to work
in his office, alongside Jason Ede. Yeah, that is right. Where is Jason Ede? Tell us that.
We never hear Jason Ede coming out to tell us what went down in those days.
Andrew Little has traversed some of the ground today. We had the Government not
saying anything about State house sales at the time of the election, and then
1918 General Debate 25 Feb 2015
miraculously having as its major focus at the mom ent the sale of State houses. We had
the Skycity deal presented as being no cost to the Government for the full monty, the
whole shebang. It was going to be absolutely free.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Not a cent more.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: “Not a cent more.” was the phrase that was used. We now
know that 14 months ago Mr Joyce knew that that was not the case. Either it was going
to be trimmed as to scope or the taxpayer would have to get the cheque book out. Then,
shortly after the election, we had both the Prime Minister and Mr Joyce softening up the
public for having to spend more money on it, getting beaten around the head by New
Zealanders about that, and now conceding that they will get a smaller convention centre.
We have not had the whole truth there, except what was dragged out reluctantly.
Then we come to Iraq. “No boots on the ground.” was the phrase. “No boots on the
ground.” was what the Prime Minister was saying before the election. New Zealanders
were understandably suspicious because Bill English, John Key, and Gerry Brownlee all
said that New Zealand should have gone to war in Iraq in 2003 as part of the coalition
of the willing. Lo and behold, those suspicions have been proven to be right this week
when, just a week after  the Prime Minister said that it is the cost of being part of the
club—which at that time meant was the “Five Eyes” club, our traditional allies the
United States, Australia, and Great Britain; that club —he now tries to reinterpret that as
being the United Nations and has been roundly criticised by the media for spinning on
that particular issue.
Then, this week, as if all of this is not serious enough, we know that he is misleading
us about Donghua Liu. In the middle of all of these controversies —Mr Willi amson
resigning as a Minister, as a consequence; Judith Collins in trouble with Oravida and
her donations from them, and the conflict of interest in her meetings with Chinese
border officials in China—he put out a statement through his staff and he omitted  to tell
us that he had a private dinner with Donghua Liu.
That sort of omission just does not ring true. He was quizzed about this in the stand -
up this week. It reads like a Clarke and Dawe script. It would almost be funny if it was
not so sad. He is ask ed whether he is misleading by omission. “Are you misleading by
omission?”, the reporter asked. PM: “No. I mean, look, at the end of the day we’re
never going to start getting into a process of saying where we had dinner.” “At the end
of the day” is one of  those catchphrases that he always uses as a filler when he is in
trouble.

items.speaker: Next he said
items.text: “I knew it was a Cabinet club dinner.” The reporter says: “Just to be
clear, last year your office denied the dinner was a Cabinet club dinner. Emphatically
they said no.” PM: “Right.” Reporter: “You’re saying it was a Cabinet club dinner?”.
PM: “Well, that’s only what I read in the paper in the weekend. People have their own
definitions of it.” Reporter: “So to be clear, was it a Cabinet club dinner?”. PM: “I don’t
know. You’d have to ask Jami -Lee Ross. He organised it.” Reporter: “But didn’t you
say it was a Cabinet club dinner?”. PM: “Well, like I say.” Reporter: “How do you
define a Cabinet club dinner?”. PM: “Well, that’s right. How do you?”. Reporter: “Well,
we don’t go to them.”

items.speaker: It gets worse. Reporter
items.text: “So you seem to be contradicting your office. You
emphatically said it was not a Cabinet club dinner.” PM: “Well, probably it wasn’t,
then. I don’t know. I don’t know the details.” Reporter: “But just moments ago you said
it was a Cabinet club dinner.” PM: “Well only because that’s what I read in the paper. If
you’re telling me it wasn’t, then it wasn’t.” Reporter: “But you were there.” The
catalogue of events where the Prime Minister has to have the truth dragged out of him
does him no credit whatsoever.
25 Feb 2015 General Debate 1919

items.speaker: Hon TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Tēnā koe Mr
Speaker, ā, ka nui te mihi ki a tātau i tēnei ahiahi. Ko tāku wāhanga tuatahi ko Te Reo
Māori hei whaiwhai haere i te aroha nui ki ahau o taku reo, ā, ka mutu ka huri ki te reo
Pākehā mō te wā. Mr Speaker, me huri ki tētahi kaupapa hei whaiwhai atu i te mema rā.
He kaupapa harikoa, kaua ko tētahi kaupapa āhua titi ki  te ngākau, he mea pōuri rawa
ēngari ko te kaupapa nui, ko te kaupapa ātaahua nei tērā ka tū ki roto o Ōtautahi, ki te
wāhi e noho nā koe, i Ōtautahi.
Ā te wiki e tū mai nei ka kitea atu Te Ao Māori e whakaeke atu ana ki runga i a Ngāi
Tahu, otirā, ngā iwi e noho nā ki Te Wai Pounamu. He aha te kaupapa? Ko Te Matatini!
He aha Te Matatini? He huihuinga ā -tāngata, he huihuinga Māori, ki te whakanui i a ia
anō. Ko te mata, arā, ko te kanohi o te tangata, tērā āhuatanga tini. Ko tērā wāhanga,
tērā kupu e mea ana, ko te tokomaha. Ē hia kē nei! Nō reira, he pai tērā whakamārama a
Wharehuia Milroy mō Te Matatini - he kohikohinga ā -tāngata, he huihuinga ā -tāngata,

He aha te mahi i Te Matatini? Ko te mahi kapa haka ka kitea mai ai ko te kapa ā -

Moana a Te Rōpū Reipa te mahi. Ka pai!
[Thank you, Mr Speaker. Huge accolades to us this afternoon. My first part will be in

switch to English for a time. Mr Speaker, to follow on from that member, let us turn to a

Next week Māoridom will be seen alighting upon Ngāi Tahu, but at the same time
upon the tribes living down there in the South Island. What is the purpose? It is the
Matatini. What is the Matatini? It is a gathering of people and of Māori honouring itself
once again. Te mata is the face, in other words, the face of a person, that aspect of the
myriad. That part, that word tini is referring to the great number, to the myriad; an
absolutely massive number. So that explanation by Wharehuia Milroy for Te Matatini is
a good one —a collection of people, a gathering of people, an assembly of people
performing from the heart.
What is done at Te Matatini? Cultural performances that will be seen will be posture

items.speaker: KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI
items.text: Thank you for the opportunity to
speak during the general debate. First of all, I would like to congratulate all my fellow
Kiwis on the new lunar year. This is a time when we all celebrate the lunar year.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: Gong xi fa cai.

items.speaker: KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI
items.text: Yes—gong xi fa cai. Yesterday we celebrated the
lunar new year in Parliament and we are attending lots of functions around the country.
The Sydney siege highlighted for us in this p art of the world that New Zealand
cannot be considered immune to the dangers posed by terrorism. Due to our distance we
may be a bit far away; however, our geographical positioning is by no means an excuse
for us to take a lacklustre approach. Our leader, the Rt Hon John Key, outlined
yesterday the brutal and unfortunate realities of the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant
(ISIL). Some recent events further highlight the threat that ISIL poses. The beheading of
journalists, who are on the ground only to re port on the current situation in that region,
and the kidnapping of hostages are some of the many serious threats that we have to
keep in mind when we discuss the serious, complex decision that the Government
announced yesterday.
25 Feb 2015 General Debate 1921
As we have seen, three yo ung teenage girls have just left the UK and have gone to
join the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria terrorists in Syria. It is a very serious thing that
we need to understand —that those guys are influencing the young generation and
asking them to join them in the Middle East and to create a threat.
Over the past few months the world has witnessed the ability of ISIL to attract, train,
and keep foreign fighters motivated. Further, as an organisation it is well armed and has
access to a constant flow of funds to it. Anyone who, despite knowing all these details,
still feels that ISIL is not a threat needs to re -examine their facts. Based on the facts
available, I am of the firm opinion that ISIL is a threat not just to the peace and stability
of the Middle East but as a region globally.
We live in an interconnected world and we have to play an active part, while
ensuring that New Zealand’s interests are taken care of. As the Prime Minister
mentioned today during question time, New Zealand’s approach is that we have to be
part of humanitarian, diplomatic, and capacity -building exercises in the region. By
doing so we are standing by the values of New Zealanders. We are taking the righteous
decision of helping support the rule of law internationally. Furthermore, w e are doing it
only on the request of the Iraqi Government, which has time and again sought
international assistance for ensuring the safety and security of its citizens.
Although I am speaking about the rule of law internationally, I now want to focus on
New Zealand. I was pleased to take over as the chair of the Law and Order Committee.
The Prime Minister recently set Better Public Services targets and I am pleased that we
are on track to achieve those. The crime rate is the lowest in the last three deca des.
People feel safe at home, at work, and on the streets.
I would also like to share the announcement made by the Hon Michael Woodhouse
increasing the minimum wage from $14.25 to $14.75 from 1 April 2015. I think the
wage rise strikes a perfect balance between the needs of employees and the ability of
employers to pay. This is what we can call a win -win situation. The annual inflation
figure stands at 0.8 percent, while the minimum wage has risen by 3.5 percent. This will
directly benefit 115,000 workers and lead to increased wages of $60 million a year. This
shows once again that we are listening closely to the needs of stakeholders and that we
are making decisions based on their needs.
Another example that I can share here of where the Government is li stening to the
community is the decision by the Minister for Ethnic Communities—

items.speaker: PAUL FOSTER -BELL
items.text: It is a pleasure to follow on from my

This weekend we have an opportunity —not so much in New Zealand, but we will

1922 General Debate 25 Feb 2015
spoilers away, for those who have not seen the first two seasons, but needless to say
these are the Machiavellian machinations of Frank Underwood, a political character. I
am not going to take a cheap shot at the Opposition, but one could make any number of

For this Government, I think it is a very positive mark of our level of c ontribution to

This morning on the Education and Science Committee we heard in public hearings
from a couple of our tertiary education institutions —the Tertiary Education

Zealand’s economy but to get better outcomes for New Zealand students, to make sure

I was delighted to hear of the efforts and work being done to boost Pasifika and

are well quipped to participate in the modern workforce and to take advantage of some

Another very positive story that we heard in that committee was around international

subsidise young New Zealanders doing courses but actually they are creating a bus iness

items.text: The time for t his debate has expired. As this is the first general
debate for this parliamentary year I just want to remind all members of Speaker’s ruling
47/1. The general debate is a type of debate that I expect to be political and impromptu,
and I think it is unnece ssary for any member to have to read a speech through the
general debate. Today I have observed three members reading their speeches and,
disappointingly, two of those members are senior members of this House. If a member
was a new member or if a member wa s to use a general debate slot to state something
quite technical I may be lenient. But in the future if a member comes into this general
25 Feb 2015 General Debate 1923
debate and proceeds simply to read a speech, do not be surprised that their speech may
well be curtailed.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
MANUKAU CITY COUNCIL (REGULATION OF PROSTITUTION IN
SPECIFIED PLACES) BILL
Second Reading
Hon ANNETTE KING (Deputy Leader—Labour) on behalf of Su’a William Sio
(Labour—Māngere): I move, That the Manukau City Council (Regulation of
Prostitution in Specified Places) Bill be now read a second time . This bill has a long
history—a very, very long gestation, indeed. On 22 November 2005 the former member
of Parliament for Manurewa the Hon George Hawkins introduced the first of these bills.
It was the Manukau City Council (Control of Street Prostitution) Bill. It was introduced
in the 48 th Parliament. The bill provided for local control over street prostitution in
Manukau City. On 7 Dece mber 2005 it was referred to the Local Government and
Environment Committee. At the time of its introduction the Hon George Hawkins
outlined what he said were the local problems relating to street prostitution in the areas
of Hunter’s Corner, Papatoetoe; t he Ōtara town centre; and the Great South Road,
Manurewa. They were concerned as a local council about the growing number of sex
workers soliciting on the street. It was not a bill —and never was—about the legality of
prostitution. That bill had been passed  some time earlier, so it had nothing to do with
legalisation or decriminalisation of prostitution in New Zealand.
So 10 years on —from 2005 until now —we are debating today the reading of a
second bill to deal with this issue. I need to tell those who are listening that so much
time has gone into this issue —probably more time at a select committee on a local bill
than at any time in the history of this Parliament. We have had report after report. We
have had evidence backwards and forwards, legal opinions g iven, the evidence of that
legal opinion given, and another legal opinion given. And in the meantime, throughout
this, the Manukau City Council disappeared altogether and was replaced by a super -
city.
The first select committee report on the first bill re commended that the bill not
proceed, and that it be voted down at the second reading. It was voted down by the
select committee on the grounds that having a local law different from national law in
respect of prostitution was unworkable. Seven members of t hat original committee have
now left this House. Those left are Pita Paraone, the Hon Nick Smith, and Metiria Turei.
Then on 11 October 2006 we had that second reading. It was voted down by 46 votes
to 73. But I have to tell the House it did not deter the  Hon George Hawkins. He came
back with another local bill, the Manukau City Council (Regulation of Prostitution in
Specified Places) Bill, and on 20 August 2010, now the 49 th Parliament, this bill was
introduced. This bill in clause 3 authorises the counci l “to make bylaws specifying
places in the district where the business of prostitution or commercial sexual services
may not occur otherwise than in a brothel or a small owner -operated brothel.” This bill
went back to the Local Government and Environment Committee.
In the 2011 election George Hawkins retired and the bill was then picked up in the
50th Parliament by the former member for Manukau East Ross Robertson. I sat on the
Local Government and Environment Committee for 2 years and I need to tell membe rs
of this House that we gave this bill serious consideration. Once again, we heard
evidence, we reheard evidence, and we sought legal advice and advice from the
Auckland Council.
1924 Manukau City Council (Regulation of Prostitution) Bill 25 Feb 2015
By the end of 2014, before the election, the committee had come to the conc lusion
that the bill was not needed. That was the conclusion of the committee. We had looked
at the evidence; that was the decision. And it was the decision for the following two
reasons. Auckland City, we were told by all the opinions we got, could alread y make a
by-law. It did not need this House to make a by -law for it. It could make a by -law to
control street prostitution. We did not need to waste the time of this Parliament making
a by-law.
The second reason was that we knew and heard that lining up b ehind this Auckland
City were a whole lot of councils wanting their by -law. So we could in theory have up
to 70 councils coming wanting their particular by -law around street prostitution. We
said that this was a nonsense. We could not have a whole lot of l ocal bills clogging up
this Parliament when there was the ability for Auckland City to make a by -law, and it
ought to get on with it. Certainly, Christchurch was one of the first that was lining up
but there were others around New Zealand. Unfortunately, t he bill was not concluded
before the House rose for the last election.
So, finally, we get to the 51 st Parliament and this bill, now in its fourth Parliament,
has reached this point today. We think it is time to stop after 10 years of Parliament’s
time and money and say to the Auckland Council: “Pass a by -law, because you can. If
that is what Auckland wants to do, just get on with the job.” The select committee
recommends that this bill not be passed and that we conclude this bill here at the second
reading, as we did with the first bill that the Hon George Hawkins introduced way back
Can I just say in conclusion that I want to thank the committees that have worked on
this bill. I say to the people of Auckland and the councils that have been invol ved that it
was taken very seriously. We looked at all the issues. We believe that we have come up
with the right solution. Also, I want to thank the three members who have promoted this
bill—as good members would promote a local bill —George Hawkins, Ross Robertson,
and Su’a William Sio, who have faithfully brought this bill and argued it for their local
community. I know that they will be disappointed that it has not proceeded but they also
understand and know that Auckland City can go ahead tomorrow if it  wishes and
prepare a by-law—

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Some councils have.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: —and, in fact, Hamilton is one of those that has, so we
know that it is possible. In fact, some of those that have joined the super -city had
already created their own by-laws.
So, I say to those former members who may be missing, thank you for your hard
work but this is going to, hopefully, be the end of this bill and the end of the time of this
Parliament dealing with it.

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: I rise to speak in the second reading
of the Manukau City Council (Regulation of Prostitution in Specified Places) Bill in my
capacity as the current chairman of the Local Government and Environment Committee.
I want to acknowledge and thank the Hon Annette King for her very detailed,
thoughtful, and good analysis of the history of this piece of legislation and its long
march and journey through the Parliamen t of New Zealand. I think the Hon Annette
King made a very good point about now being the time for Parliament to bring this
matter to an end and to encourage and, in fact, invite the current Auckland Council, if it
wishes, to pass the by-law that it so clearly can, should it wish to do so.
About 25 years ago I was manager of a business called Protector Safety. It had a
branch in Hunters Corner in Papatoetoe in Manukau City as it was then. I can assure
members that even that long ago we as local business pe ople were having to contend
with the issues of street prostitution and particularly the issues that related to tidying up
25 Feb 2015 Manukau City Council (Regulation of Prostitution) Bill 1925
the mess that was there every morning as we opened up the business for a day’s trading.
We had to sort of clear away the goings -on fro m the night before. So I have an
enormous amount of sympathy for the business folk of Hunters Corner and other parts
of South Auckland where street prostitution has been, without doubt, an ongoing issue
for many, many years.
But, as the Hon Annette King has so clearly pointed out, the reality is that after years
of deliberation, after years of getting advice, after years of consultation, and after years
of hearing from every kind of expert possible on these matters, we as a committee came
to the very clear decision and the conclusion that, in fact, Auckland Council already has
the power to create a by -law should it so wish. Indeed, other councils around the
country have done so —Hamilton City Council has been mentioned —and before the
amalgamation of the Auck land super-city, Rodney District Council had in fact passed
its own legislation, which under the rules of amalgamation and the way Auckland City
has been set up actually stand in place today.
The Local Government and Environment Committee concluded that it was
absolutely possible for Auckland Council to regulate street prostitution should it so
wish, and that if it were to do so, it would not be in any kind of contravention of, or
inconsistent with, the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act or indeed the Prostit ution Reform
Act, which has been cited as a reason by those people who would want this Parliament
to make special legislation on this matter. They think that it may in some way be an
inhibitor or a roadblock. In fact, it is not; the advice we have had is v ery clear that it is
not. It is very possible for Auckland City to do so, if it wishes, in a way that is not
inconsistent with the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act and not inconsistent with the
Prostitution Reform Act.
The Local Government Act 2002 specific ally allows local authorities to make by -
laws to protect the public from nuisance; protect, promote, and maintain public health
and safety; minimise potential for offensive behaviour in public; and regulate trading in
public places. Under each of those hea ds, there is more than sufficient scope for
Auckland City, should it wish, to pursue a by -law in this area. In fact, this very day,
representatives of Auckland Council appeared before the Health Committee to tell us
about by-laws it had made to regulate solaria and sunbed operations in Auckland City. It
strikes me that Auckland City has the capacity—and, in fact, the history—to regulate by
by-laws all manner of behaviour and business and human activity. It seems to be able to
do it with great gusto and grea t enthusiasm on a whole range of other subjects. Why it
has chosen not to do so on this matter defies my understanding.
Many of the complaints about street prostitution relate specifically to issues relating
to noise, to littering, and to slow -moving vehi cles, which is usually referred to as
kerbcrawling, and, of course, they relate to issues relating to disorderly behaviour.
These are actually all matters that are able to be dealt with under the existing by -laws
that the Auckland Council has available to it.
After all this time, after all this history, the select committee of the 51 st Parliament
came to a unanimous conclusion that this bill should not be passed. The Hon Annette
King made the very good point that if that was not the case and, in fact, if t his
Parliament did pass this piece of local legislation, then we would be inundated with
requests from all other local territorial authorities seeking us to pass the same type of
legislation in a way that I think would be a gross misuse of this Parliament’ s time and
resources, particularly given that the opportunity for by-laws already exists.
So we come now to the 51 st Parliament, nearly 10 years on from the time when the
first iteration of this bill was introduced by the Hon George Hawkins, all those yea rs
ago. It is time, I think, for this House to support the recommendations of the 51 st
Parliament’s Local Government and Environment Committee, and support the
1926 Manukau City Council (Regulation of Prostitution) Bill 25 Feb 2015
recommendation of the committee, passed unanimously, that this bill not proceed. That
is the course of action that I commend to the House, and I do so with confidence that it
will be supported by the vast majority of members across the House. I commend the
committee’s report and its recommendation to the House.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Assistant Speaker. I
stand on behalf of New Zealand First to disagree with both previous speakers. I stand on
behalf of New Zealand First to explain why we disagree. It is  not that we do not
understand. It is not that we do not understand the advice that was given to the Local
Government and Environment Committee way back in 2005 and 2006, nor is it that we
do not understand the advice that was given to the select committee  only last year. We
understand that we had a member on that select committee, Andrew Williams.
However, it is our view —it is our view —that the people of Manukau have been let
down by this Parliament. It is our view that the select committee could have done  more.
Although it might have recommended that this bill not go forward, it could have made
other recommendations.
I note very clearly that the two previous speakers have relied on advice that
Auckland Council can already create a by -law, and that is true . That is absolutely true.
As a person who was part of the submission process with regard to the Rodney District
Council and the laws and the by -laws that were created then to create areas where this
industry could do its business without interfering with the everyday lives of the other
citizens in that area, I know that what Mr Simpson has said is true. The Rodney District
Council had very strong laws. Actually, of all the amalgamated councils, the Rodney
District Council had the most conservative by -laws around this particular industry. It
was threatened on several occasions with being taken to court because it wanted to
protect and fit within the current legislation, but it also wanted to make sure that its
citizens, who pay the rates in that area, had a level of protection. So we created those
by-laws. And then the Rodney District Council was absorbed into the super -city of
Auckland and, because the super -city of Auckland’s absorption has not worked as
quickly as perhaps was imagined, those by -laws still stand in just the 46 percent of the
land mass of Auckland that was Rodney District.
However, it is a cop -out, quite frankly, to rely on what is a true statement —a
theoretically true statement—that a by-law can be created, because it absolutely can be.
But then it must be enforced. I think the other thing too that is interesting about that is
that as a member of the Rodney Local Board, I knew that the by -laws staff had to go
around every local board, once we had this amalgamation of the super -city, and had to
ask about prostitution as a business and what sorts of controls we would want to put in
place to flatten out the by -laws across the whole of Auckland. And there is one of your
other things—I assume that the select committee had a briefing on the fact th at this is
now about flattening out by -laws across the whole of Auckland. Any by -law created or
any issue that you might have in what is now Manukau City inside the super -city would
actually have to be assumed across the whole of the city.
But what was interesting about that consultation was that the Auckland Council staff
told local board members: “You don’t need to create a by -law. You don’t need to create
a by-law because they are hawkers, so really this is just about hawking. So we can just
use the current by-law”—which is a hawking by-law—“and then we can actually go and
issue these people with a ticket.” Let us just have a think about the practicalities of that.
What has just been said is that this bill wastes 10 years of this Parliament’s time, but
this is a real issue to real people who are just trying to go about their daily lives. So,
apparently, there is a hawking by-law already on the books and we can send out by-laws
officers at 3 o’clock in the morning, 4 o’clock in the morning—[Interruption]

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER

member for those members’ rudeness. Thank you.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: That is all right, Mr Assistant Speaker. We can send by -laws
officers at 4 o’clock in the morning to go and give a ticket —to go and fine the

Apparently—and it is a truism —we can send out a by -laws officer and give the

It is all very well and good to say: “You can.” and it is all very well and good to say
that you have the ability to, but it is another thing completely to say how that will take
place. How? You can, but how do you do it? There is absolutely no practical thought
inside the select committee’s response to this bill. In all three parliaments that dealt with

of New Zealand? Where was the will to address street prostitution? It is not only the

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: We’ve already got it. Just go to the police.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: So, here we go—we have got it again. We are going to leave it
to the people on the street to have to deal with it. This Parliament brought in a law —
[Interruption]; and those gentlemen are apparently very supportive of it —and then it
dumped it out there for the people of New Zea land to deal with. When the people of
New Zealand come back to their Parliament and say: “Something’s wrong with it and
we would like Parliament’s assistance to actually fix it.”, apparently it is in the too -hard
basket. Apparently, it is 10 years of waste d time, which is what the two speakers before
me said.
These are citizens of New Zealand, who pay our wages, who have come to this
Parliament and said that something is wrong with a piece of legislation. They are not
asking for that legislation to be overturned—nobody here is. What they are asking for is
recognition of a problem and for us to come up with a solution, and this House is
supposed to be here for them.
So although this bill will fail, New Zealand First will support it. We will support it
because it actually is an issue that this House needs to address. We—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Actually, it’ll end up wasting the House’s time.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: It needs to be addressed. We refuse to actually slap these
citizens in the face and say: “It wasn’t important enough. We decided not to put any
other solution in here or any other recommendation in here. We decided to just say it
was 10 years of our time. Too bad. Go away and deal with it yourself. Ring a by -laws
officer at 3 in the morning. Call a police officer and go into court, and take all that time
out of your day and your life because this Government and this Parliament decide that it
is not worth our time.”

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: It is—in contrast with the previous speaker, Tracey Martin—
with a certain amount of relief that I rise to take a call on this bill, the Manukau City
Council (Regulation of Prostitution in Specified Places) Bill. This is the second ti me
that legislation like this has come before this Parliament. As has been very well outlined
by Annette King earlier, there has been 10 years of consideration of the detail of this
issue. This Parliament has spent a huge amount of time listening to the co mmunity and
considering these issues. It has not in any way, as the previous speaker may have
suggested, been a flippant dismissal of the concerns of the community. There has been a
rigorous process of looking at the appropriate role for responding to this  problem. My
understanding is that the Local Government and Environment Committee has possibly
1928 Manukau City Council (Regulation of Prostitution) Bill 25 Feb 2015
spent more time on this issue than it has on pretty much any other piece of legislation in
recent years. This has not been a flippant dismissal.
The Green Party was on the committee and supports the unanimous decision of that
committee for this bill not to proceed further. I am also aware that some people will be
really unhappy with this recommendation. I went and met with some people at the
committee and we hear d the submissions. I have real empathy for their situation. We
were told of businesses losing money, residents losing sleep, parents fearing their
children were having to see and hear things that children should be protected from. I
absolutely believe that they are valid concerns. This is a problem that needs a solution. I
sincerely wish to see those concerns resolved.
I would commend anyone who is listening to this debate to go and read the full
report of the select committee to find out the detail of wha t we considered. It came
down to whether legislation was the way to solve those concerns. It was the unanimous
view of the committee that legislation is not going to solve this problem. The problem
needs a solution, but legislation is not the answer. We li stened and we really engaged,
but, ultimately, our role is to consider whether legislation is the appropriate response
and, in this case, whether a local bill that applies to only one area —albeit an area that
covers a third of our population—is appropriate.
Local bills need to address local issues and not national issues. We heard previously
that several other councils —in response to lobbying, I must admit, initiated by the
Manukau city councillors —indicated that they may see this as an area of concern and
want to have a response to it. So it is quite clear that there is ambiguity about whether
this is a local issue. We considered all the evidence and came to the conclusion that the
problem was best solved at a local level, as well as potentially looking at  other
legislative solutions on a much wider level through the Local Government Act.
It was the contention of Manukau and the then Auckland City Council that they
could not regulate street prostitution by existing laws. We disagreed with that solution
and we have heard that assessment. We noted that the Rodney District Council had
specified that street -based sex workers meet the definition of “hawkers” and, as such,
are regulated by its by-laws on trading in public places and require an operating licence
from the council. Further, Hamilton City Council has created a prostitution by -law that
restricts the location of brothels, sets out signage requirements, and also prohibits
soliciting in public spaces and within view of public spaces. So we have evidence t hat
by-laws are able to be used to regulate this.
The committee heard from a previous member that there is still the outstanding issue
of enforcement. You can put a law on your books but can you enforce it? The question
that the committee then had to cons ider was whether that issue would still exist if we
legislated. The answer was yes. We would still have the problem, if we legislated, of the
police needing to enforce the legislation or to enforce the by -laws that we would enable
to be created by this legislation. That problem would not go away. In fact, we also were
told that the police currently have the ability to prosecute on summary offences, which
covers a wide range of behaviours such as suspected disorderly behaviour, indecent
behaviour, threatening or indecent language, and wilful damage to property. They can
arrest without warrant when they have good cause on any of those grounds already. All
the behaviour that was described to us by businesses and residents fitted those areas of
concern.
So the police have the ability already to arrest without a warrant. Why would we
create a duplicate law for one specific area of the country, or even enable by -laws to
duplicate that provision when obviously the problem is around the resourcing of the
police to e nable them to do that? If that is the problem, then we encourage the
community and we encourage the council to be lobbying the Government for increasing
25 Feb 2015 Manukau City Council (Regulation of Prostitution) Bill 1929
resources to the police to enable that to happen. But we would go for a more
empowerment-based model ou rselves. Clearly, the answer is not in legislation, in
duplicating existing powers.
Another reason we were told for putting forward this legislation was that it was
expensive to introduce these kinds of by-laws. Therefore, the council wanted Parliament
to spend the time—and it has spent 10 years —to develop legislation. We acknowledge
that maybe there is an issue around the cost of developing by -laws and the processes of
developing the regulations under that, but that is not an issue specific to prostitutio n or
for the Auckland Council. That is a much wider issue that should more appropriately be
dealt with through a wider piece of legislation, and we would encourage any council to
negotiate with its member of Parliament for such legislation to be put forwar d. So we
are not dismissing that concern; we are just saying that this piece of legislation is not the
way to deal with it.
We were also told that enforcing by -laws can be resource intensive and that proving
an offence can be difficult. Again, we believe that these challenges would remain if this
legislation was introduced. There is nothing in this legislation that would solve that
problem. Evidence has always been a really difficult thing in this area. In fact, one of
the reasons for the introduction of t he Prostitution Reform Act was as a public health
measure to create an environment where we did not disincentivise the use of condoms,
because prior to that legislation passing, condoms were used as evidence in prosecutions
against sex workers. We would not want to see a return to that situation.
In some ways legislation is presented as a simple way to fix this problem. There is no
simple way to fix this problem. But we would say that the discussions and the work that
have been happening at the local level , post the introduction of the bill this time, have
seemed to be really positive. There is work happening at the moment. It follows on from
the Ministry of Justice’s report recommendations from 2009, where it went into the
Manukau community and investigate d the best possible response to solving these
acknowledged problems. It came up with a really long list of actions that it
recommended take place in that community, like having toilets open at night with
lighting, putting in extra rubbish bins put in, and having control around the sale of
alcohol in the area.
I do need to point out to the members in this House, and to anyone listening, that
although we were told that all of those measures had been implemented, what we found
was that they had not been, and that some had been implemented for only a short period
of time and had then been unwound. Really, this community has not been served well
by its council. The appropriate place for it to be solved is in the community. We believe
that more resources from thi s Government to support the community to do that would
be appropriate, but not legislation.
