items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: I move, That the Parental Leave and Employment
Protection (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amendment Bill be now read a third time . I
thought I would never ever get to say those words, because what a wild ride this has
been—what a wild ride this has been. This bill was pulled from the ballot almost 3 years
ago, in April 2012. Actually, it was the Thursday just before Easter. I recall it very well
because a lot has happened since then. Can I, at the outset, thank all of the parties that
have contributed to making sure this bill did in fact get to its third reading. I want to
thank the Green Party, New Zealand First, the Māori Party, United Future, and Mana,
when it was in Parliament, for ensuring that these families, families of newborn babies,
had their issue debated in our Parliament. It is only because of the support of those
parties that we have got to the point where we are.
But I want to reserve my greatest thanks and gratitude to my Labour colleagues. It is
the Labour Party that had the cour age and —yes, Mr Key —the guts to stand up for
families when no one else would. It was my Labour colleagues who, at the height of a
global financial crisis, understood that this was where the brighter future really did lie
for New Zealand. It was my Labour c olleagues who, despite the fact that the
Government was running a scare agenda of saying that nothing could be spent on
anything positive, actually decided to turn the tables and trust New Zealanders’ instincts
and say: “Yes, New Zealanders will back a pos itive initiative that will make a real
difference.”—and did they ever. New Zealanders got this. They were able to
demonstrate that it was the Labour Party that is completely in tune with the thinking of
decent, hard-working New Zealanders.
Despite the fact that the Minister of Finance at the time over -inflated the bill, said it
was going to cost $500 million, and tried to frighten the New Zealand public into not
putting families first and not supporting children in this way, it backfired. The New
Zealand public sensed that the Minister of Finance was exaggerating. They knew he was
wrong and they knew in their hearts that this was the right thing to do. The New
Zealand public was in tune with the New Zealand Labour Party and the New Zealand
Labour Party was in tune with the New Zealand public.
We know this because there were a couple of polls that were conducted, and I
imagine that the National Party did more than a couple of polls —I think it was polling
regularly on this issue. It is the only reason that it has actually capitulated on this,
because it knows of the public’s support. When Television One went out and surveyed
25 Feb 2015 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 1931
about a thousand New Zealanders and said “It’s going to cost $500 million —do you
want it or not?”, 65 percent of respondents said “Yeah.” Even at that exaggerated
level—[Interruption]—yes, they did. And the members opposite still do not believe it,
but the poll said 65 percent wanted paid parental leave extended to 26 weeks, despite
the fact that the Government was exaggerating the cost of i t and threatening a financial
veto against it. So from the get-go there has been this sort of controversy and that sort of
degree of push-back from the National Party opposite, because it did not trust the public
on this, it did not want to prioritise families, and it just did not get how important it is.
When it came to the select committee process, we had almost 4,000 submissions
come to the Government Administration Committee on this. That is how strongly
people felt about it. And 99.6 percent of those submissions were in favour of extending
26 weeks’ paid parental leave to all the families who are currently eligible. Only 0.04
percent opposed it —0.04 percent opposed it. I remember one of those submissions
really well for all the wrong reasons, because B usiness New Zealand, in its desperation
to try to support the National Government’s opposition to this bill, decided to come and
argue in front of the select committee that the reason it opposed this bill was that if
women had 6 months away from paid emplo yment, they would completely forget how
to do their jobs and they would need complete retraining, and this was going to be a big
imposition on business. It was going to cost them a lot of money, and that was why it
should be opposed.
Well, I think Business New Zealand very soon crawled back into the cave that it had
crawled out of on that occasion, because we had to point out to them that actually the
law, as it stands, already allows women to have 12 months’ leave from their jobs, and
then they come back and do their jobs quite successfully. That was the level of
desperation from the supporters of the National Party’s opposition to extending paid
parental leave. That is how desperate it did get.
The first deception happened in the select committee on this  bill, in this wild ride,
because the National Party MPs, faced with seeing the strong support that this bill had
and knowing how bad it was going to look for them, decided that they needed to try to
turn this round somehow. So they came to me and asked for an extension of the time for
the Parental Leave and Employment Protection (6 Months’ Paid Leave) Amendment
Bill to stay in the select committee, so that they could have some time to talk their
colleagues into supporting it. I took that in good faith, and  I probably should not have.
A very wise woman told me, quite some time ago: “Never trust a Tory.” Never trust a
Tory, she said, and I should have remembered that. I forgot it at precisely the wrong
moment, and I trusted the Government MPs when they promis ed me that if they
extended paid parental leave, it would be done in a bill in my name. That is the
commitment they gave me. They lied. They reneged on that commitment—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: Sorry, Mr Assistant Speaker —they misled me. They deceived
me. They misled and deceived all of the families who were relying on an extension of
paid parental leave to 26 weeks.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: And they laugh about it.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: And they laugh  about it, because they think that is clever. They
have played politics with this bill from day one, but they have forgotten —because of
their arrogance —that they are in fact playing politics with people’s lives. They are
playing politics with those very im portant first few months of a baby’s life, and I think
it is disgraceful.
We came to the second reading of the bill, when it came out of the select committee,
and there was more drama. I do not know whether people recall this, but the National
Party whips  made a mistake when they cast the Māori Party vote, and they had the
1932 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 25 Feb 2015
Māori Party voting against the bill instead of in favour of it. That meant that the bill
could not proceed. When Pita Sharples came down —when he realised what had
happened and he came do wn to try to correct the vote —he got taken outside by the
National Party whips, he got taken outside by some of the Ministers, and he got bullied
into not correcting the vote. It did, over time, get corrected, but that is part of the
interesting political story about this bill.
We moved on—we did eventually get that vote corrected —and we moved on to the
Committee stage, and, wow. Was that the National Party’s finest hour, or what? It
filibustered a bill that would give 26 weeks’ paid parental leave to fami lies—
filibustered it in order to try to stop it from going ahead. In the National Party’s finest
hour it put up Mike Sabin to do four speeches lecturing New Zealanders on how to raise
children. I am just going to say that again. It had Mike Sabin stand up on four occasions
to filibuster this bill and lecture New Zealand families on how to raise children
properly. Do you feel proud? Does the National Party feel proud about that? Well, I
hope that it will feel proud about that particular issue in the months to come.
So after all of this, what have we achieved? What we have achieved —what Labour
and our allied parties have achieved—is we have pushed the Government into extending
paid parental leave to 18 weeks over the course of the next 2 years. We know we hav e
pushed the Government into that, because Bill English looked right down the barrel of a
TV camera when that bill came out of the ballot and said: “It is not a priority for us to
extend paid parental leave. Even when we are in surplus we will not extend p aid
parental leave.” And look what has happened. But today the story has got even more
interesting, because now the Government is promising to deliver what my bill does
today, but not do it in my name because it is still playing politics. It has promised t hat it
will do it in a bill in its own name. Thank you.
Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE (Minister for Workplace Relations and
Safety): I do appreciate the opportunity to take a call on the third reading of the Parental
Leave and Employment Protection (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amendment Bill. As it is
a members’ day it is customary that members of the executive do not tend to speak on
members’ bills, and I do appreciate that I have been given the opportunity to do so.
Firstly, I want to talk a little bit about what we have heard from the person
sponsoring this bill, Sue Moroney, and also, as the Minister for Workplace Relations
and Safety, to lay out what the Go vernment does intend to do by way of improving and
extending paid parental leave to parents over the next year or two. I will say this about

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: she is certainly passionate about this issue. I have no doubt about the
authenticity with which she ha s championed the issue of paid parental leave, but I do
worry that she has mixed the politics and the passion to such a degree that it is
impossible to work out which is which. Nevertheless, I do want to touch on a couple of
elements of what she said.
I heard her say that it was her Labour colleagues who have, in her words, “had the
guts to support this bill”, and that is perhaps true, except that what she did not say was
that that was not the case when they were in Government. When money was sloshing
around and Labour was spending money like drunken sailors, locking in structural costs
that this Government has had to deal with, the very canny Dr Michael Cullen —of all of
the things that they could have done, of all of the passionate things that they could h ave
supported, increasing paid parental leave to 26 weeks at a cost of who knows what, but
several hundred million dollars is the best estimate, was not part of the Labour
Government’s agenda. It is very interesting that, as this is a member’s bill —and
knowing that it is not possible for members’ bills to have that kind of financial impact—

items.speaker: Ms Moroney would say
items.text: “Right, now we are in Opposition it is time to increase paid
parental leave”.
25 Feb 2015 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 1933
When we are in the most straitened times that this country has seen i n 80 years,
suddenly it is a priority for Labour, when, in previous years, they did not see raising the
length of paid parental leave to 26 weeks as a priority. Lions in Opposition —lions with
other people’s money when it does not have the fiscal costs of t he decisions that it
wants this Parliament to make—but lambs in Government.
Indeed, there are some other statements that have been made by Ms Moroney about
what the Government did or did not say about paid parental leave, and I want to make it
very clear that the Government always said it was prepared to extend paid parental leave
as and when fiscal conditions allowed. It is really important to understand that the fiscal
conditions did not allow that. What did the Government do? An amount of $500 million
has been bounced around as a possible cost, but I think that overly exaggerates the cost
of Ms Moroney’s existing bill. Let us remember, we are not debating the original bill.
This is not a matter of principle and passion, because Ms Moroney herself has wat ered
down her own bill. Why? Because the goal is no longer to extend paid parental leave to
26 weeks; the goal is to embarrass the Government. The goal is to expose the
Government, and that is the politics of this. That is the politics that is interfering with
the passion.
The Government, in these straitened times, the toughest conditions in 80 years —
which was left with the legacy of structural deficits for 10 years, which we have seen
halved, despite the impact of the Canterbury earthquakes —has come up wi th around
half a billion dollars of measures to support children and their families. We have seen
that in the free general practitioner visits for under -13s. We have seen that with the
breakfast in schools programme.
Do you know what the most disappointing thing about the Labour Party in
Opposition was? It campaigned in 2008 on the fact that this Government, should we
have the privilege of taking the Treasury benches, would gut Working for Families and
would gut interest-free student loans. Do you know what made it most angry in the 49 th
Parliament? We did no such thing. Through those vulnerable periods we made sure that
the supports that were locked in place stayed for our most vulnerable.
The Government does intend to increase paid parental l eave. Not only is it prepared
to do that, but it has already locked in, through Budget 2014, the fiscal appropriation to
do just that. It is necessary now to change the legislation to give effect to that, and it is
my intention to bring a Government bill t o the House in about June of this year, and
have it passed this year, for effect on 1 April 2016, as we have already appropriated. It
will increase the duration of paid parental leave for those parents who are already
eligible for it. It will go to 16 week s in the first year and then to 18 weeks thereafter.
But it is going to do more than that. It is going to broaden the range of people who are
eligible for paid parental leave. At the moment, the legislation provides, I think, for a
very one-dimensional view of employment and a one-dimensional view of employees. I
think what we know now is that employment relationships, but also parenting
arrangements, have changed significantly in the last generation or two. Firstly, people
work in more than one role. They work in different ways: they may be self -employed,
they may be contractors, they may have multiple employers, and they may have moved
recently, before expecting a child.
None of those conditions are currently met by the existing legislation, or by the bil l
that Ms Moroney has introduced. The Government will change that. The Government
will extend the range of parents who will be eligible for paid parental leave to include
those different working arrangements, to include multiple employers, and to include
those who have been working for their employer for only 6 months, which would
actually rule them out under the current regime.
1934 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 25 Feb 2015
It is also going to recognise the fact that parenting arrangements can be different as
well. I take, for example —and I acknowledg e the Māori Party intervention into this
particular part of the policy that is being developed —the concept of whāngai, or
traditional Māori adoption, which is not recognised presently in the law, and will be
when the Government introduces the bill into the  House in the middle of the year. That
will be very important, and I want to acknowledge the Hon Te Ururoa Flavell for his
intervention to ensure that that very longstanding traditional means of bringing up
children will be met in this scenario.
What we ha ve is a passionate member, who has no concern for fiscal impact,
introducing a bill that I believe she introduced with the best of intentions—although it is
a little hard to untangle the politics from the passion —who then watered it down when
she realised that she would not have the numbers and, actually, that the Government
was coming up with a better arrangement to support families by increasing the duration
of the support and broadening the nature of the relationships and the number of
employment relationships that would be covered by it. I do acknowledge her.
But the Government takes this very seriously. Support for parents and enabling
mothers, in particular, to re-enter the workforce is a very important part of growing this
economy and ensuring that people stay connected with the workforce. I should also add,
actually, that the bill being introduced in June will allow parents to keep in touch if they
are on paid parental leave. At the moment, if you go back for a single day you lose your
entitlement to paid parental leave, but that is often not practical for people who are in
highly skilled jobs, who want to keep in touch with training and development, or who
need to cover for leave. There will be sensible provisions in the bill that will enable that
to occur.
The National Party will not be supporting Ms Moroney’s bill. It will be introducing a
very sensible range of measures that will deliver a better outcome for parents. I look
forward to Labour’s support when that bill is introduced.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: It is my pleasure to take a call in this final reading
of Sue Moroney’s Parental Leave and Employment Protection (Six Months’ Paid
Leave) Amendment Bill. Perhaps I need to start by correcti ng the record. The Minister
who just resumed his seat, Michael Woodhouse, stood and asked the House why, if
Labour cared so much about this issue, it did not do anything for paid parental leave
when it was in Government and running a Budget surplus. I find  it extraordinary that
the Minister who claims to have responsibility for this area does not know the history of
paid parental leave. It was introduced, Minister Woodhouse, by the previous Labour

items.speaker: Government. Let me repeat that again
items.text: paid parental leave wa s introduced by a previous
Labour Government. Can I just point out that at the time it was introduced in 2002,
National opposed the introduction. It opposed the introduction of paid parental leave
when at that time in 2002 we had a surplus of $2.5 billion.  It was absolutely financially
responsible for Labour to say we have the ability to do this and it is the right thing to do,
and it was National that opposed that we did that.
We did not just introduce it; we extended it. In 2004 we looked to expand and e xtend
it again. National again opposed it. At that point we had a surplus of $5.6 billion. Again,
it was possible to do it, we did in it a fiscally responsible way, and it was the right thing
to do. Perhaps if the Minister missed all of those points, he mi ght like to be reminded of
the National Party’s positioning at that time, because it was not opposition just on
monetary grounds or fiscal grounds. It is not that the members stood up and said:
“Lovely idea, but we really can’t afford to do it right now.”,  because at that time they
were begging for tax cuts. They knew that we actually could financially afford it. That
was not the rationale for which they opposed it. They opposed it because they
ideologically did not believe in it. They ideologically did not  believe in it. Anne Tolley
25 Feb 2015 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 1935
in 2002 said: “This legislation … shows how the Labour -Alliance Government is stuck
in the radical feminist era of the 1960s and 1970s … and is completely out of touch with
women of the 21 st century…”. Anne Tolley never supporte d paid parental leave. Those
were her words.
Nick Smith said that the draft bill was a “dumb bill”. Paul Hutchison said that it was
cementing State dependency rather than incentivising individual responsibility —what,
for an infant? I do not even know what  he means by that statement. Judith Collins in
2004 said it was another example of this Government using taxpayers’ money to try to
win some votes. I find it absolutely rich for that Minister to try to tell this side of the
House that we have never believe d in paid parental leave when it is that side of the
House that is only supporting it for the pure politics, because when you strip it away, it
still does not believe in the concept of supporting women and newborn children when
they are unable to work at the most vulnerable period of a child’s life.
Members talked about dependency, being out of touch with women, and harking
back to a feminist era of the 1960s. Well, actually, if it is harking back to feminism, that
is not something I would apologise for. B ut the point is that that Government is
extending paid parental leave only because of the hard work of Sue Moroney and the
support of parties like the Greens, Labour, and New Zealand First. That is why the
Government eventually shifted.
If we want to talk  about anyone being out of touch, it would have to be the
Government. Only yesterday a report was released by Growing Up in New Zealand, a
longitudinal study that 7,000 children are part of. It is the most in -depth study we have
seen of children. It tracks them from birth to adulthood. That report has found that more
than 50 percent of New Zealand mothers experience hardship between late pregnancy
and the first 9 months of their child’s life. I repeat that: 50 percent of New Zealand
mothers experience some level of hardship between late pregnancy and the first 9
months of their child’s life. And here we are, with some arguing that we cannot afford
to do more to support those families in the most vulnerable period of their child’s life.
That is not something I am saying off the cuff without research and evidence.
You do not have to look at the UN’s feedback—of course it supports breastfeeding in
the first 6 months. That stands on its own. But organisations like the Brainwave Trust
have long argued that if you  want to invest anywhere, invest in those first critical
months of a child’s brain development. Their connection with a parent is critical. It is
what determines whether or not they are able to build trusting relationships in
adulthood. It determines wheth er or not, for instance, they will experience some of the
behavioural issues that we then grapple with as taxpayers further down the track.
Conduct disorder, something that is connected to whether or not a child forms those
trusting relationships and bonds , costs the taxpayer $1 million —$1 million—per child.
We have been shown what we need to do about it; yet, we turn a blind eye.
We literally cannot afford not to do things like what Sue Moroney has proposed in
this bill. So if we want to talk about cost, I can tell you that that is where the real costs
exist. If we want to talk about being in touch with what new parents are experiencing,
we should be looking at the evidence, like the longitudinal study Growing Up in New
Zealand. It is interesting that when  mothers were first interviewed before they gave
birth, the mothers’ plan was to go back into the workplace, to use up what paid parental
leave they had, and then return. What the study found was that a number of mothers
would use up that paid parental lea ve, then they would try to use up all their holiday
leave, and they would then try to take unpaid leave. They would do everything they
could once their baby arrived to stay with their child as long as they could. That was
when mothers started exiting the w orkforce. When they used up all that leave and
realised that they were not ready to go back, they exited the workforce.
1936 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 25 Feb 2015
So if that Minister was really serious about mothers trying to maintain bonds with the
workforce, he would recognise what the evidence was telling him and maintain that link
via decent paid parental leave. That is what would make a longer term bond to the
workforce, and that is what he should be looking at and listening to. That would
demonstrate that he was truly in touch with what New Z ealand families are
experiencing.
That study was the kind of information that we, as the Labour Party, looked at when
we established our Best Start policy. Not only did we ensure that paid parental leave in
our policy would be 26 weeks but after that we s aid that for the rest of that year we
wanted an additional contribution for those families to ease the burden that almost any
family, no matter what their financial circumstances, experiences in that first year of
their child’s life. We absolutely stand by  that policy. It is the right thing to do and it is
the most cost-effective thing to do.
I want to use the last moments of my contribution to pay respect to Sue Moroney and
the work she has done on this bill. The audacity of the Minister —to claim that she  has
confused politics and passion. There is no harder thing than to compromise as a
politician, and, yet, Sue Moroney saw an opportunity. She could not get 6 weeks’ leave
for every family—or try to at least do that for families who experience a premature birth
or a multiple birth or who have a child with a disability—so she compromised her bill in
order to try to make gains for at least some families. That demonstrates that this was
always about the issue more than it was about the politics. It was always about the issue,
and it is extraordinarily disappointing that that Government has been unwilling to
accept that sometimes when you see a good idea you should vote for it, regardless of
who puts it up.
Labour votes with National on good ideas. That is what  we do. That is what a good
Opposition does. What a good Government should do is recognise that a good idea can
come from the Opposition as well. I am saddened on behalf of New Zealanders that the
Government did not recognise that. So let it be said and le t it be on the record that when
that side of the House comes before this Parliament with a bill that will allow those
families to access greater paid parental leave, it was Sue Moroney who did that for
them. There is no way that that Government deserves any recognition.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The next call is a split call. I call
Sarah Dowie—5 minutes.

items.speaker: SARAH DOWIE
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker, for
allowing me to take this short call on the Parental Leave and Employment Protection
(Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amendment Bill. I would like to start out by acknowledging
the sponsor of this bill, Sue Moroney. Like the speakers before her, I do acknowledge
the intention she has in bringing this bill to the floor of the House, and the spirit of the
bill, but, unfortunately, this Government cannot support it on the grounds of fiscal
responsibility. I also  want to respond to the claims made by the member opposite, Ms
Ardern, who pointed to a number of dissenting opinions in 2002.
I stand here and say, as part of this Government, that we do support the spirit of the
bill—we do support paid parental leave—but we disagree as to the fiscal constraints and
how we are going to implement it. As such, talking about the spirit of the bill, we are
saying that this is not a case of one size fits all, and, as a Government, we have to
balance competing priorities and lo ok across the board as to the well -being of children
and their mums. In that vein I want to reiterate, as the Hon Michael Woodhouse did,
that this Government is extending paid parental leave from 14 to 16 weeks on 1 April
this year, and then, again, to 18 weeks on 1 April 2016. That meets the fiscal
responsibilities of being in Government, and it will be a very good help to those
families having children.
25 Feb 2015 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 1937
But, again, in response to the spirit of the bill, we are looking at measures across the
board, and I want to take time to talk about one of them that I, as a mother, found
extremely helpful. I am talking about the $20 million extra invested into maternity
services and Well Child services for new mothers and babies. For me the Well Child
services were a go dsend. I, as a new mum, relied heavily on the support of my family
but also the experts, such as the community nurses who worked for Plunket. They
provided me with advice as to how to deal with children, and how to bond properly
without getting too concern ed about the colic I faced or the other issues I had to work
through. Just in terms of that example, although paid parental leave is being extended
by this Government and is of help, the advice that those nurses gave me rounded out
that support and was inc redibly well received by me. It helped me enjoy the time I had
with my newborn baby.
I also want to talk about this Government extending free general practitioner visits
and prescriptions to children under the age of 13. Again, from a cost perspective for  a
family, to be able to take your child to the doctor and not worry about the cost is
extremely important. You do not need to worry about the cost. You certainly do not
worry about the burden that you could be putting on your finances. Again, that support
from GPs to enable your child to be seen, to get the treatment that they may need, and to
help them to flourish into the future is another example of an all -rounded package that
this Government is bringing into force. Again, I stand here as part of this G overnment
and I say we support the intent and spirit of the bill. Again, I do acknowledge the
member who sponsored this bill for her passion, but there are fiscal constraints when
you are in Government and, as such, we cannot support this bill.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call Jami-Lee Ross—5 minutes.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: There is a bit of a theme developing righ t
now on the Opposition benches. The theme from the Labour Party seems to be that
National is so mean that it will not let the Labour Party pull out the credit card to spend
up large. That is effectively what the Labour Party is saying.
We have to be clea r when we talk about paid parental leave that there is one party
sitting in the House right now that is extending paid parental leave, and that is National.
I do not know whether the Labour Party was listening during the Budget last year, but
the National Government has announced, and has enacted, changes to extend paid
parental leave in New Zealand. The National -led Government has implemented a
package worth $500 million to support families. Included in that package are two
extensions of paid parental leav e, which will eventually take paid parental leave out to
18 weeks. I have heard the Labour Party today say that extending paid parental leave to
26 weeks is affordable. I am sure it would also try to find an argument that extending it
to 52 weeks would be affordable, and then it will go to 2 years, 3 years, and 4 years.
The problem with the Labour Party—and we found this during the election—is that it
thinks everything is affordable. During the last election campaign the spending
promises from that side of  the House amounted to $30 billion. Those members think
everything is affordable. This side of the House, instead, does things in a measured way.
We support families, we support New Zealanders, but we have to recognise that every
time the Government spends money to support New Zealanders, it also comes out of the
pockets of New Zealanders. I think the last thing that New Zealanders would want is for
any Government to put New Zealanders into more debt, which the other side wanted to
do, and to have to raise taxes, which the other side wanted to do, when there is a more
affordable and measured way to do it.
We are supporting families. Families in New Zealand are getting paid parental leave
extensions. As part of our $500 million package as well, families in N ew Zealand are
going to have the ability to send their children to the doctor for free, up to the age of 13.
1938 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 25 Feb 2015
Families in New Zealand, because of the National Government’s changes that we have
enacted, will see parental tax credits extended. Families in New  Zealand, because of the
changes the National -led Government has enacted, are seeing more funding going into
early childhood education and more funding going into welfare changes to support
families in this country. We have the track record to do it.
I feel a little sorry for Sue Moroney. I feel that she has been hung out to dry by her
party. The Labour Party has found in the last election that its promise is unaffordable;
that its promise is not one that the Labour Party was able to sell to New Zealande rs, and
she has been left to hold out this bill—which actually says nothing at the moment. It has
a title, it has a commencement date, and it has a clause that outlines the principal Act
that she wished to change, but it has nothing else in it. If she had some honour, she
would have asked the Business Committee to drop the bill, but she was hung out to dry
by her party.
We are extending paid parental leave. We are enacting changes for New Zealanders.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I am offended by that
misrepresentation by that member, and I would like him to withdraw and apologise.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Well, I am not quite sure what the
point of contention is. There has been quite a robust exchange across the benches. What
specifically are you objecting to?

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: I am objecting to the member saying that I was hung out to dry by my
party when, in fact, it was his party that filibustered the bill—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: No, no. [ Interruption] No, that is
not a point of order.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Is this a new point of order?

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: It is a new point of order. Can I seek your clarification? During Mr
Ross’ last contribution he said that if Ms Moroney had any honour, she would have
asked for the bill to be withdrawn. Is that parliamentary language?

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: That is certainly parliamentary
language.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: Sometimes the truth is hard to believe. I was interrupted in my
flow, but I was outlining the fact that the National Government has been supporting
families. When members on this side of the House go out and knock on doors, stand in
the main streets of their cities, and talk to New Zealanders about wh at they want, they
want a country that is affordable for their children to live in. They want a country that
supports their children in their time of need but does not tax them and rack up debt to
pay for it. They want a Government that lives within its me ans. They want a
Government that provides proper housing for New Zealanders—we are doing that. They
want a Government that provides good -quality education services for their families —
we are doing that. They want a country that provides health services for their families—
we are doing that.
Families in New Zealand are far better off because of the changes implemented in
the past 6 years. The Labour Party may wish to go out and say that the National
Government is not doing enough for families, but our track r ecord speaks for itself. We
are extending paid parental leave. We are doing so in a measured way. That is what this
country deserves and asked for. It passed its judgment in September last year.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: I rise again to offer the Green Party’s support for Sue
Moroney’s member’s bill to extend paid parental leave to 26 weeks, even though, sadly,
the Parental Leave and Employment Protection (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amendment
Bill does not contain that p rovision any more because it was previously voted down by
this Government. I do want to take just a moment to properly commend Ms Moroney
25 Feb 2015 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 1939
for the work that she has done in the very long process of shepherding this bill through
the House and providing an op portunity for New Zealanders to express their
overwhelming support for paid parental leave and the care of the smallest members of
our society. That support has been overwhelming, and the Green Party appreciates your
work and all of the compromises that yo u have made to try to get even the barest
amount of provision through to those New Zealanders who were consistent on what
they asked for through the select committee process.
We have just heard from the previous member, Jami -Lee Ross, that when National
members are out on the streets they hear New Zealanders asking for everything but paid
parental leave. I would ask that member to go back and look at the submissions, and
consider the parliamentary process and our democratic process, which presented this bill
and asked New Zealanders for their opinions. I would remind that member that there
were 3,809 submissions made on extending paid parental leave to 26 weeks. I would
just remind that member again that 3,795 submissions out of those 3,809 submissions
supported the extension to 26 weeks—that is, 99.6 percent of submissions said that they
wanted 26 weeks’ paid parental leave. And even the other 0.4 percent were not
necessarily against the bill; they just had some concerns around some aspects of it, for
some of them. So, you know, this is completely overwhelming support from the
population, saying that they wanted 26 weeks. To say that when you are out on the
streets you are not hearing any support for this bill —I find that hard to believe. I refer
you to the Parliament of which you are a member and ask you to listen to the
democratic voices coming through this Parliament. I remind every member of this
House that we are here and we set up these processes for people to participate for a
reason—to inform us in th e decisions we make in this House. To ignore the views of
New Zealanders when making those decisions does a discredit to this institution and to
every single member of it.
I also go back to the process, to reflect on some of the process of this. We have h eard
a lot of politicking tonight. It has been suggested by the Minister for Workplace
Relations and Safety that the member Sue Moroney has offered passion, but that it has
been confused with politics. I really do want to challenge that —not that the Labour
Party needs the Greens to support it or defend its honour. But it really does just seem
horribly unfair and misrepresentative to me, when the member extended the submission
time and the consideration within the Government Administration Committee to enabl e
the National Party members of that committee, who were overwhelmingly convinced by
the evidence, to go back to their caucus to try to get support for this bill. That then
turned into the Government putting something forward in the Budget that was entirel y
different, which I absolutely supported. We voted in support of it. I totally agreed with
the extension of the provisions of paid parental leave to groups that were missing out.
That was a really important initiative. But it was not what Parliament and t he people of
New Zealand had been discussing. There was one clear submission that asked for that to
happen, and I supported it, but the others did not. The others were saying that 26 weeks
was the fundamental thing that they wanted addressed, and that is w hat this bill has
been seeking to do.
There was a huge amount of accommodation made by that member. And then the
Government turned round and sought to make personal political gain from it. Then we
hear that now Sue Moroney, in looking at the numbers in th is House, went and spoke
with the ACT Party about whether it would seek to have this bill go back to the
Committee stage to debate some of the substance again. She was able to convince the
ACT Party member of the need for 26 weeks and the democratic process and the request
from New Zealanders. When the National Party heard that that was happening, it called
the member into the Prime Minister’s office and said: “You can’t support this bill. To
1940 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 25 Feb 2015
stop you doing that, we’ll put forward and deliver the content of  this bill. But you can’t
support it through a Labour initiative. We’ll do it.” That is politics. I have to say that
that deeply offends me. I am not in this House to play political games. I would have
thought that every member of this House was here to de liver for New Zealanders —to
listen to New Zealanders and to deliver for them. That kind of politicking is not doing
our job, in my opinion. It is playing politics, and doing a disservice to New Zealanders.
Good on David Seymour, as a new member, for actua lly listening to and hearing the
arguments, and seeing what the provisions of the bill had been reduced down to by Sue

items.speaker: Moroney
items.text: ensuring 26 weeks for when there was a premature birth, or when there was a
child with an impairment that would entitle a person  to Government-funded disability
support, or when there was a multiple birth. So 26 weeks’ leave for those people —I am
so pleased that Sue Moroney’s bill has prompted the delivery for them, because who
could not think that there was a clear need for those families to have time out of the
workforce, to be able to bond with their babies, to take care of health needs, to just be
able to cope.
The submissions that we heard during the select committee —again I want to thank
those submitters because they were tea r-evoking submissions for every single member
on that committee. We heard of people who had missed the early years of their child’s
life and had to look at photos of their babies to remember what they looked like at that
time, because they had had to go ba ck to work. We also heard of people who had
managed to get 10 months to spend with their babies and who had bonded with them
and found a love of parenting, even though they actually had not wanted to be a parent
before that. They had managed to use that ti me to bond and connect, and find joy. We
can only imagine the flow-on benefits of that time to the parent, to the family, and, most
important, to the child. In the submissions that we heard —to get to the point of what
this is all about —the evidence was overwhelming that the benefit of 26 weeks’ leave is
that it facilitates bonding and attachment between parent and baby, and improves the
learning and the development of the baby, the health outcomes for mothers, babies, and
children. The World Health Organiza tion recognises 6 months as the minimum for
breastfeeding.
This provision supports families and ensures stability of their incomes. It allows
choice for women in maintaining workplace attachment, and it updates our employment
conditions to recognise the contemporary world that we live in. Most of us have
families, and it is appropriate for workplaces to adapt to that. Twenty -six weeks makes
it easier for employers to manage time out and substitution of workers. So this bill, the
26 weeks’ leave provision, is not just a matter of what would be nice. For $110 million,
which is the cost of what this would be, the return to us as a country was judged by 99.6
percent of submitters as worthwhile. It is a shame on this Government that it has
subverted the democratic process and is refusing to deliver that.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: It is an honour to be able to stand this afternoon and
speak on the Parental Leave and Employment Protection (Six Months’ Paid Lea ve)
Amendment Bill. I, like others, also want to commend Ms Moroney. She is not here
right now, but I just commend her intent.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member cannot refer to
the absence of a member.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker. I was trying to speak in
acknowledgment of the member, who is not here, but I do want to acknowledge—

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: For goodness’ sake, Alfred, learn the rules.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: —OK—the sponsor of the bill. It is a bit of a mean spirit there.
I am actually acknowledging the sponsor of the bill and her intent. That is what I want
to do, because the intent is right.
25 Feb 2015 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 1941
It is of interest, I know, to all MPs to be able to have their own member’s bill pulled
out of the ballot and to have it presented to the House. It is important to us. The reason
why it is important—and I know that later on tonight in the House Tracey Martin’s bill
will be debated—is that the ability to have your own bill drawn out of the ballot means
that you can become the champion of a cause that is important to you. That is what
members’ bills allow you to do, especially for those in your community who advocate
for the importance of a bill. So I take nothing away from the sponsor of this bill and the
importance that the issue of this bill tries to address around paid parental leave and
employment protection.
With that, I acknowledge the intent, like the  intent of all members who are
honourable members in this House. However, where we begin to differ is in the how.
How do we ensure that we meet that demand and that need in the community? I want to
just make some comments, because there have been previous speakers in the House
who talked about the previous Labour Government and what it did when it introduced
paid parental leave. They talked about the extension of that paid parental leave. I want
to just go over those points. For instance, in 2002 paid paren tal leave went from 10
weeks to 12 weeks —that was in 2002. In 2004 it went from 12 weeks to 14 weeks,
which is what it is currently, until its extension later this year from 14 weeks to 16
weeks. And in 2016 it will go from 16 weeks to 18 weeks.
The reason I make mention of that is that those increments of change are the same
increments of change that this Government is also making. They are the same
increments of change, by 2 weeks, so it is no different from what the Labour
Government did in its time to increase paid parental leave by 2 weeks in that period of 2
years, from 10 weeks to 12 weeks, and then from 12 weeks to 14 weeks. For us, it goes
from 14 weeks to 16 weeks, and then 16 weeks to 18 weeks. So I make the point that we
are making the same responsible judgments, which we think are absolutely important as
well.
The other thing I want to make mention of is that there was talk about this
Government being mean -spirited in this. It is my understanding that the Hon Ruth
Dyson, who was a Minister at that time, was also presented with a brief about extending
paid parental leave even further, and at that time it was declined. So, again, under a
Labour Government there was no intent to try to increase it even further, even though
petitions were made on th e same issues relating to parental care and responsibility.
Again, under a Labour Government, it was not increased.
The other point made by Ms Ardern, the previous speaker, was in regard to a Labour
Government looking towards introducing bills that it fel t were important to New
Zealanders. Can I mention that this was talked about by a member who was previously
here in Parliament, the Hon Tariana Turia, when she talked about the issue of Whānau
Ora. I want to make mention of this in the House because it is not often talked about,
but when she talked about Whānau Ora at a number of conferences, she made mention
of the fact that it was under a Labour Government —under the leadership of Helen
Clark—that she introduced the idea. She talked about Whānau Ora being important for
Māori and their families. She talked about having a better way to meet their needs and
to have self-determination so that they could be self -determining for themselves, for the
hapū, the iwi, and for the nation of Māori all together. It was a  Labour Government
under Helen Clark that declined —she declined —to even introduce this into the
conversation. Yet it was under a National Government that Whānau Ora was not only
introduced, with a commitment of over $137 million over 4 years, but we now ha ve
three commissioning agents—two for Māori; one for Pasifika.
That is the care and concern —that is the difference between a National Government
and a Labour Government that seeks to create continuing dependency, rather than
1942 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 25 Feb 2015
saying to those communities, in particular, that it can find a way to help support them. I
make mention of that to say, again, what this National Government is doing to make a
difference to families in our community.

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: Tell us a bit more about the bill.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: Let us talk a little about this bill for Mr Lees -Galloway,
because he probably has not read the bill. Changes to the parental leave framework —
here is the difference that we are making. We are going out and having a con sultation
process to talk about how we can change the bill in an appropriate way that is fiscally
responsible—as was talked about before on the other side of the House —and that
ensures that the changes that we make meet the different complexities that diff erent
families have in this day. Over 900 submissions have already been put forward and,
from that, the changes will allow for greater access and increased flexibility.
Here are some of the key proposals that we are introducing, which are really
important and which we believe supersede the intent of this bill and instead show what
we are doing to support and care for families and children in New Zealand. The key
proposals are as follows. We are extending parental leave payments to people in less
regular work, such as seasonal and casual workers, those with more than one employer,
and people who have recently changed jobs. We are extending parental leave payments
to primary carers providing permanent foster care akin to adoption, such as Home for
Life parent s. People who have permanent guardianship, biological fathers, and
grandparents caring for grandchildren will be eligible, provided they meet the work test
criteria. Employees will be able to work limited hours or days and keep up skills
development during their paid parental leave. We are allowing workers who have been
with their employer for more than 6 months but less than 1 year to be entitled to some
form of work and unpaid leave. These are some of the things that we are doing and that
we believe are m aking a difference to families. We believe that that is the way that we
are showing we care.
The reason why we oppose this bill is that we are increasing paid parental leave from

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Mr Ross says it is not snarky, and yet his contribution was the

items.speaker: BRETT HUDSON
items.text: I rise in opposition to this bill , although, as my

items.speaker: DENISE ROCHE
items.text: It is with regret that I  rise to take this call on this bill
because I see it as yet another lost opportunity. It seems that every time I speak in the
House it is about lost opportunities.
This was a great bill. I pay tribute to the sponsor, Sue Moroney, who brought a bill to
the House that was a call for 26 weeks’ paid parental leave. I pay tribute to her skilful
shepherding of this legislation through the meandering corridors of Parliament and the
process, the frequently Byzantine mechanisms, you have to go through to get a pie ce of
legislation back into the House. I refer particularly to sending it to the Government
Administration Committee instead of any other committee, which I thought was a very
good tactic, and then to compromise —to go through an incredible compromise with the
Government—and attempt to reduce the scope of the bill so that 26 weeks’ leave applies
specifically to families who have had multiple births or those who have had births
where their children had suffered health or disability issues. I think that was ve ry
skilful.
So today, as we come to the third reading, we have a gutted bill, as the previous
speaker, Brett Hudson, outlined. I think “guts” is the word of the day, and I would
suggest that this bill has certainly been gutted. We bring this bill back and  it has been
eviscerated, essentially, and that is a tragedy. We know for a fact through various
research—research that has been canvassed; we have used the entire resources of
Parliament through the select committee process to look at the benefits of paid  parental
leave—that investment in paid parental leave to 26 weeks or beyond can stimulate the
economy even during a recession. That is according to Australian research.
We know that we are not keeping up with other countries. We are 24 th out of 25
OECD countries for our leave provisions on paid parental leave. If we want to attract
skilled workers in a global labour market, then we need to ensure that we have policies
and leave provisions that will attract those skilled workers to contribute to our econom y
here in New Zealand.
The benefits to first -time parents accessing paid parental leave and to their families,
to their children in those first few months, are well canvassed. We know that the
bonding with families means that there are fewer cases of neglect and abuse of children.
We know that children who have had their parents with them in the first year of their
lives have better cognition and fewer behaviour problems, which means that we save
money down the track. Investment in paid parental leave is certainly an investment in
the future, which is quite a change from the short-term thinking we see in this House.
We know that paid parental leave is good for all of us, and yet this Government has
allowed the bill, the brave bill that Sue Moroney brou ght to this House, to be
completely and utterly gutted. I have to say that Sue Moroney can take credit for the
fact that in the last Budget announcement this Government has actually moved on paid
parental leave at all. The fact that it will this year exten d paid parental leave from 14
weeks to 16 weeks and then next year to 18 weeks is to her credit. And it is to her credit
that the Government was able to see that it was going to lose votes if it did not shift on
this, because there are thousands of New Zealanders who want better provisions for paid
parental leave. It was also Sue Moroney’s bill that meant that this Government has

decided to shift on how paid parental leave can be applied, and to extend the categories
that it can apply to.
So although we ar e voting on a bill that has been gutted, has been emptied, and is a
shell of what it was, Sue Moroney can take credit for shifting this Government a few
tiny steps in the right direction.

National started to understand that it was out of touch, that it was on the wrong side of

items.text: The paid parental leave bill got to select committee and

25 Feb 2015 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 1949
The National Party has at every turn, from when paid parental leave was first

Budget 2014 provided a comprehensive package of measures focused on young
people and those who need the help the most. What this Government is doing is

because benefits had increased; child poverty was decreasing because of job creation.
So that is why we are modernising paid parental leave. We are modernising it in relation
to modern working arrangements. This is why I do not support this bill

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: I rise to talk to the Parental Leave
and Employment Protection (Six Months’ P aid Leave) Amendment Bill at its third

fact that this Government has done m ore for parents and children than any other
Government in recent memory, including paid parental leave.
This obsession that somehow only the Labour Party has the moral high ground to
hold a view on paid parental leave is absolute nonsense. This party has campaigned on
extending paid parental leave, and we got a huge endorsement from this country
because of it. What I have struggled to accept and watch from members on the other
side of the House, particularly from the Labour Party, is an absolute, almost pr ecious,
sense that unless their view of how paid parental leave is be applied, it does not matter,
and, therefore, it does not count. Well, it does count. This party has promoted it and has
got it through the last Budget, and it is delivering real value in  terms of family support
in this country.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Don’t be mean-spirited; come on.

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: It is not mean -spirited. That is far from the truth. This is a party
that is committed to paid parental leave, has campaigned on it, and has delivered real
outcomes for New Zealand. Spend, spend, spend —that is what we get from the Labour
Party. Well, guess what? It is not yours to spend. You have not earned it. The hard -
working people of New Zealand have earned it, and they have afforded us the privilege
to spend it on their behalf.
The Government has said all along —as my good colleague said earlier, and, I think,
very effectively—that we are prepared to extend paid parental leave, but in a way that is
affordable. We can afford m ore when we can afford more, and we were very clear in
Budget 2014 that over this financial year we would make some adjustments in that
regard.
This is a Government that is focused on delivering a comprehensive package of
practical measures—practical measures that deliver real value to New Zealand families
25 Feb 2015 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 1951
right here, right now. It is not some utopian view whereby you can provide everything
for everybody. This is a package that delivers real value that we can talk to. We have
lifted paid parental leave to 16 weeks, and then we will extend it beyond that, to 18
weeks. For our young families we have provided the opportunity to have free GP visits.
This is real stuff, OK, and when you get the extreme anger that we hear expressed on
the other side of the House because their particular view of paid parental leave does not
progress, I think it is a nonsense.
We can talk to a record that is very, very strong for families in this country. In only a
couple of months’ time we will be able to extend paid parental leav e out to 16 weeks,
and then, of course, next year from 1 April we will extend it to 18 weeks —18 weeks.
This is not a Government that is not supporting families. That is 18 weeks’ paid parental
leave from next year, and we will increase the parental tax cre dit by $70 a week to $220
a week. They smile and say: “Oh, that’s not good enough.”, but that is real money in the
pockets of families in New Zealand, at a time when we have got a whole lot of
competing objectives. We can, I think, talk quite confidently t o this country about our
record of achievement. That is why, quite frankly, when we took this to the country, we
got the result that we got last September. I have appreciated the opportunity to spend a
few moments talking about why our approach is the righ t one and why I will vote
strongly against the bill that is front of us tonight. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: Sorry about that momentary
interruption. I had to pick up my  pen that I dropped in stunned surprise, actually, at the
contribution from that member. I am unable to recall his name. He is a new member and
perhaps that is why he gave such a confused, rambling speech. I intend to put the facts
on the record so that th at member will not come into this House and make things up,
and talk about voting against a bill that earlier on this very day his Minister committed
to introducing. He calls other parties confused. That member will be voting for this
legislation when it is in the name of National. That will be the only difference.
He calls Labour financially irresponsible. This legislation would have cost $6 million
for the three target groups that Sue Moroney narrowed this bill down to in an effort to
get some compromise  and support for the most vulnerable families, so that they could
have the additional support they need. When Sue Moroney offered that compromise to
National, costing $6 million—a quarter of what National is spending on referendums for
flags—that member and his party said no, and tonight his name will be on the record for
voting against extending paid parental leave to families of premature babies, to families
who have multiple births, and to families who have disabled children or children with
specific hea lth needs. There are not many other families who are more deserving of
additional support than those. If there had been, the member could have added them at
the Committee stage of this bill, but, instead, he is voting against those families.
That is one of the best things about our Parliament. The name of every member of
Parliament is on the public record alongside how they voted. The member who split his
call with the member who has just resumed his seat gave the second speech that he has
given in Parlia ment. The first one was his maiden speech, and that was his second
contribution. I want to congratulate him on the birth of his baby. I know that it is a
delight to him. I have seen him out and about in Christchurch showing off his baby, and
well-deserved too. Tragically, he talked a load of nonsense as well —beautiful baby;
terrible speech. He said: “If we don’t have the money, it’s all just talk.” Well, what
about in 2002? In 2002 the Labour -led Government Budget surplus —I know that is a
strange word for the National Party to hear, but we did it every year—was $2.5 billion.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: Wasted the surplus.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: Mr Bishop should remember that —$2.5 billion. He wrote the
speeches for the National Party front bench to  come in and say: “You’ve got a surplus.
1952 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 25 Feb 2015
Why don’t you give tax cuts?”. And we said: “Because there are better priorities —
higher priorities.” So we introduced paid parental leave in 2002 with a $2.5 billion
surplus, and what did the National Party do? What did the National Party do? This party
comes in here making stuff up like: “We’ve always supported paid parental leave.
We’ve always supported families and babies.” Every single member of the National
Party voted against the introduction of paid parental l eave in New Zealand. We were
finally taking a step towards getting up to speed with the rest of the world that we like
to compare ourselves to. Every other country that we like to compare ourselves to has
got paid parental leave. In 2002 we had a $2.5 bill ion Budget surplus, and National
voted against it.
In 2004 the Labour -led Government extended paid parental leave, and that year we
had a $5.6 billion surplus. Eat your heart out, Bill English —a $5.6 billion surplus. And
what did National do then? “Oh, we  don’t have the money.” It had the money for tax
cuts, but it said it could not afford to extend paid parental leave. And exactly the same
thing happened in 2006. We became, in 2006, the first country in the world to have a
form of paid parental leave for the self-employed. That is a very good thing because we
have a lot of self -employed people in New Zealand. We broke new ground. What did
National do? For that similar -sized Budget surplus—listen to those words; you will not
hear them much while there is a National-led Government—National voted against it.
So Mr Doocey and Mr Muller, do not come into this House making stuff up, because
the Budget surplus and the voting record of your party are on the public record. And
what you said —“If only we could afford  it. It’s all just talk. You’ve got to walk the
walk.”—is absolute nonsense.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: Laila made you do it.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: Mr Bishop knows it because he wrote those rubbish speeches
that Bill English and his colleagues set up. I want to congratulate Sue Moroney on her
attempt to get paid parental leave extended. I think New Zealand families would have
welcomed this. In fact, I can say that with a lot of confidence, because I chaired the
select committee that considered t his bill and there were over 3,000 submissions to the
bill, and 99.6 percent of the submissions on this legislation totally supported it. About
0.5 percent of submitters said that there are some good things and some bad things
about it, you know —that there were perhaps some tinkering measures that should take
place before they would be 100 percent supportive of it. One single submitter —one
single submitter out of over 3,000 —opposed it, and that was a tragic submission,
actually. It was tragic. The young man  who presented the submission clearly had been
obliged to on behalf of his employer, and clearly did not want to.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: The National Party, I think.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: And the National Party, I am sure, strongly encouraged  him.
It could find only one person in the whole country. He said that one of the difficulties
with giving women paid parental leave was that, generally, after having a baby and
taking time off they forgot what their jobs were, and they had to be completel y
retrained—so it is total amnesia. I am sure Mr Doocey would know about it. I am not
sure whether his wife would share that view; I doubt that she would. She looks pretty on
top of things to me, actually, and she has recently had a baby. But this submitte r said
that women who had a child should not have time off from work because when they
went back they would have completely forgotten it. He also forgot that, of course, at the
moment we have an entire year’s entitlement in the law for unpaid parental leav e, so
this bill is actually just filling that gap of absence from the job with some money to
support the family. For a lot of families, of course, it makes the difference between them
being able to choose, genuinely, to stay at home with their newborn baby  and have the
25 Feb 2015 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 1953
attachment that Mr Doocey has clearly had experience with, which everyone in this
House will know is so important.
Listen to the health experts and the family support experts who say that breastfeeding
for the entire time of 6 months, if pos sible, is best for the development of the baby. Of
course, the stress and pressure of having to work in a job part -time or full-time as well
as having a new baby is big. So the more genuine choices we are able to offer families
by giving them the financial  support that can make that choice a reality, the better it is
for New Zealand families. So I am just stunned not only that the National Party fought
so pathetically against this bill by filibustering on a member’s bill for hours and hours
and hours when i t had been watered down, if you like, or tailored, to a meagre $6
million a year. It was a compromise on a plate that National could have accepted, so that
those who might be considered the most vulnerable of families, the most in need of that
additional support because of the pressures they are facing, could be the ones who got
the first additional assistance.
This is less money than it is costing the Government —taxpayers—to move the
Treaty of Waitangi one block from Archives New Zealand to the National L ibrary of
New Zealand. That is costing $6.7 million —a very good spend, I am sure. It is a whole
block that the Treaty is moving —$6.7 million. The implementation of paid parental
leave for this targeted group would have cost $6 million. As I have said, it i s a quarter
of the amount of money that the National Government is going to spend on referendums
for a flag.
Simon O’Connor: And how much in the second year? And the third and the fourth
and the fifth?

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: Mr O’Connor, you should take a call and explain to your
constituents and the country why your name is going against extending paid parental
leave. Sue Moroney did her best to introduce—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: I am sorry to interrupt the member,  but her time has
expired.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: I seek leave to table a letter to Government MPs,
asking them to support this bill to extend leave to 26 weeks—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought for that purpose.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: Can I just describe who the letter is signed by and who the letter
is from?

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: You have described the letter. Leave is put for that
purpose. Is there any objection? The document will be tabled.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Dr PARMJEET PARMAR
items.text: Thank you for the opportunity to speak on
Sue Moroney’s bill. This bill is to extend the paid parental leave entitlement of 14
weeks to 26 weeks. It was good to see that the member who spoke before me, Ruth
Dyson, acknowledged that National gave tax cuts when we had money, because we do
not believe in taxing and spending. I acknowledge that newborns’ and mothers’ health
and development benefit from a period of absence from work without worrying about
income. This also helps with the balance that is needed in family life and work life, and
also help s settling in, with the changes coming to the family with the birth of a
newborn.
The National-led Government continues to invest in different public services to help
children and families. The Government has already announced changes to parental leave
provisions as part of Budget 2014. As for the changes coming soon, we know that the
current entitlement of 14 weeks is going to be increased to 18 weeks in two stages.
From 1 April 2015 the current entitlement of 14 weeks is going to be increased to 16
1954 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 25 Feb 2015
weeks, and on 1 April 2016 leave provisions will be extended to 18 weeks. Not just that,
but from 1 April 2016 parental leave payments will apply to more workers: those who
have just changed jobs, seasonal and casual workers, and workers with more than one
employer. Also from 1 April 2016 primary carers, Home for Life parents, and other
carers with similar permanent arrangements will be able to access paid parental leave.
For babies born on or after 1 April 2015 the Government is increasing the parental tax
credit from $150 to $220 a week and is extending the payment period from 8 weeks to
10 weeks.
Parenting is an important and also complex issue and a process that can be stressful
and difficult. Raising children is enjoyable, I know, but it can be difficult no  matter how
many children one raises. It is important for children to have their parents or caregivers
or their family with them, especially as a newborn. I acknowledge that. Parenting is an
ongoing commitment, but families do like to keep that balance bet ween the time a
person spends at home and the person’s commitment to their field of work. It is
necessary that we take into account both sides and find this balance, and that is what the
National-led Government did. It announced that paid parental leave ex tension from 14
to 18 weeks.

items.speaker: Stuart Nash
items.text: Give women a choice—don’t speak on their behalf.
Simon O’Connor: With everyone else’s money.

items.speaker: Dr PARMJEET PARMAR
items.text: Yes, it is everyone else’s money. Paid parental leave is
a Government-funded entitlement. It is one of the uses that the taxpayer’s money is put
towards; hence we must use this money effectively. The paid parental leave programme
is a great initiative and it is important that we make it as effective and  efficient as
possible. But we need to operate at an affordable level. The extensions announced by
the Government are optimal for both family life balance and affordability.
I will share my own experience. Just like many others I did not want to stay away
from work for too long as I wanted to be an active contributor in my field of work. As
well as this, I know the opportunity to bond with my children is limited. This is why I
truly believe, and have learnt, that it is the quality of time that you spend wi th your
children, not the quantity of time that you spend with them.
The family structure is changing. Our families are becoming diverse and our needs
are changing as well. Therefore the Government is also developing further changes to
ensure New Zealand’s parental leave framework reflects current working arrangements
in today’s diverse family structures. To do this, a discussion document was released in
July 2014 seeking feedback on the Government’s proposals to enhance and modernise
parental leave. Almost 900 submissions were received, and those submissions are under
consideration currently. The Government aims to put these changes in place by 1 April
The Government continues to stand with New Zealand families and children. The
National Gov ernment is known for delivering value for our taxpayers, and is always
striving to deliver more for families and children. The Government is doing a number of
other things to help children in our communities, like extending free general practitioner
visits to children aged under 13 and free immunisation against rotavirus. It is about
fiscal management and balance. We do not support this bill.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: I would just like to congratulate
that last speaker, Parmjeet Parmar, on a very fine speech, which was representative of
somebody who has intelligence, integrity, and a desire to make a difference, unlike the
speaker before her, Ruth Dyson, who attacked her wh en she was speaking and tried to
make it personal. That is a disgrace from that member from Christchurch from the
Labour Party, who has not got the ability to debate in this House like that last speaker
has. It really is something that is the nature of thi s Parliament. I would like to also
25 Feb 2015 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 1955
congratulate Mr Matt Doocey as well. I thought he gave an excellent speech. I thought
he was right on the mark there. He talked about families, commitment, making things
work, and how there is that time and desire to do s omething by the Government for
families. I thought his speech was brilliant, and I thought that for a new member coming
in that speech was a real speech of integrity as well. I think those last two National
speakers can be very proud of the way that they h ave not played politics with this issue.
They have talked about it and they have worked through the issues in a constructive and
balanced way, just as the Government has. I also think it is important to acknowledge
Sue Moroney here today. She has put a lot  of work into the Parental Leave and
Employment Protection (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amendment Bill. Sue is also from
Hamilton, and I know that this is something she is passionate about. Whenever we have
debates in Hamilton she brings it up, and I would lik e to commend her on that. I think
that she has shown passion within that area.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Always a gentleman.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Yes, yes! No, I do. I think she has done a good job on that, and
it is a shame that some members of this House try to play politics with the issue rather
than actually look at what is going on and work towards getting long -term solutions that
everybody can work with and that are in the best interests of New Zealand families.
I think that is the most important thing, because we all want the same thing. Nobody
in this House wants to deny New Zealand families the best start that they can have. That
is part of being in this House; it is the future of our country. Of course, we want that. Of
course, everybody will work within their own ways to do this. Did you say something,
Mr Nash?

items.speaker: Stuart Nash
items.text: Are you going to cross the floor and vote for it?

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Mr Nash wants me to cross the floor —it is more likely Mr
Nash would cross the floor this way and vote against the bill, but that will not happen,
will it, Mr Nash? I am sure that cosy seat there is just too nice to do that. The fact of the
matter is that all members of this House will feel the same way. It is a matter of b alance
and of what can be done constructively within the Government. This Government has
made changes in regard to paid parental leave. We are working towards making more
available for those in that situation, and towards giving our youngest and our bright est
and our families the best opportunity we can.
There was one point that was raised by the previous Labour speaker: she mentioned
the surpluses that Labour had encountered when it was in Government, and that is true.
It had great economic times. It did not have a world recession. It did not have to rebuild
our second -biggest city. It had great economic times, and it was probably set up by
some great policies before that. It also took New Zealand into recession a year before
the rest of the world, but we have to forgive it for that, because it did not know what it
was doing. It was just following the economic policy that it had learnt, that was inherent
to its beliefs. It had the opportunity then to extend paid parental leave, but it did not
happen, did it? Did it happen under Labour when it had the money there? No, it did not.
But then the provision comes into this House and Labour makes it an issue now. And I
think that is sad, because Sue has spent a lot of time on this bill. Sue really did mean
well, and it is disappointing that Labour has not reflected that in her role in Labour now.
I think that is an indication that it does not believe in what it is doing. I am disappointed
for you in that regard, Sue. I think that Labour had that opportunity; it did not do it. We
have been in more difficult economic times, and we have still made moves in that area.
OK, it is maybe not what everybody wants, but we have to take the steps that we can.
This is a balanced approach.
In summary, I would just like to say tha t everybody in this House will, no doubt,
want to see the best for our families and our children. There is no doubt about that. This
1956 Parental Leave etc. (Six Months’ Paid Leave) Amdt Bill 25 Feb 2015
bill is part of that process of getting the best for our young children and our families.
There are going to be some change s. There is a programme ahead in the Government
that has reflected a number of Government initiatives that will deliver for our young
people going forward. I would like to thank everybody who has been involved in this
bill. Thank you.
A party vote  was called for on the question,  That the Parental Leave and
Employment Protection (Six Months' Paid Leave) Amendment Bill be now read a third
time.
Ayes 60
New Zealand Labour 32; Green Party 14; New Zealand First 11; Māori Party 2;
United Future 1.
